For the duration, you sense the presence of magical effects within 30 feet of yourself. If you sense such effects, you can take the Magic action to see a faint aura around any visible creature or object in the area that bears the magic, and if an effect was created by a spell, you learn the spell's school of magic.

The spell is blocked by 1 foot of stone, dirt, or wood; 1 inch of metal; or a thin sheet of lead.

You drive a spike of psionic energy into the mind of one creature you can see within range. The target makes a Wisdom saving throw, taking 3d8 Psychic damage on a failed save or half as much damage on a successful one. On a failed save, you also always know the target's location until the spell ends, but only while the two of you are on the same plane of existence. While you have this knowledge, the target can't become hidden from you, and if it has the &Reference[invisible apply=false] condition, it gains no benefit from that condition against you.

Using a Higher-Level Spell Slot. The damage increases by 1d8 for each spell slot level above 2.

description.value:
You create a sound or an image of an object within range that lasts for the duration. See the descriptions below for the effects of each. The illusion ends if you cast this spell again.

If a creature takes a Study action to examine the sound or image, the creature can determine that it is an illusion with a successful [[/check ability=int skill=inv dc=@attributes.spell.dc]] check against your spell save DC. If a creature discerns the illusion for what it is, the illusion becomes faint to the creature.

Sound. If you create a sound, its volume can range from a whisper to a scream. It can be your voice, someone else's voice, a lion's roar, a beating of drums, or any other sound you choose. The sound continues unabated throughout the duration, or you can make discrete sounds at different times before the spell ends.

Image. If you create an image of an object—such as a chair, muddy footprints, or a small chest—it must be no larger than a 5-foot Cube. The image can't create sound, light, smell, or any other sensory effect. Physical interaction with the image reveals it to be an illusion, since things can pass through it.

You shape-shift into another creature for the duration or until you take a Magic action to shape-shift into a different eligible form. The new form must be of a creature that has a Challenge Rating no higher than your level or Challenge Rating. You must have seen the sort of creature before, and it can't be a Construct or an Undead.

When you shape-shift, you gain a number of Temporary Hit Points equal to the Hit Points of the form. The spell ends early if you have no Temporary Hit Points left.

Your game statistics are replaced by the stat block of the chosen form, but you retain your creature type; alignment; personality; Intelligence, Wisdom, and Charisma scores; Hit Points; Hit Point Dice; proficiencies; and ability to communicate. If you have the Spellcasting feature, you retain it too.

Upon shape-shifting, you determine whether your equipment drops to the ground or changes in size and shape to fit the new form while you're in it.

You touch a creature and magically remove one of the following effects from it:

  • 1 &Reference[Exhaustion] level
  • The &Reference[Charmed] or &Reference[Petrified] condition
  • A curse, including the target's Attunement to a cursed magic item
  • Any reduction to one of the target's ability scores
  • Any reduction to the target's Hit Point maximum

description.value:
You create the image of an object, a creature, or some other visible phenomenon that is no larger than a 20-foot Cube. The image appears at a spot that you can see within range and lasts for the duration. It seems real, including sounds, smells, and temperature appropriate to the thing depicted, but it can't deal damage or cause conditions.

If you are within range of the illusion, you can take a Magic action to cause the image to move to any other spot within range. As the image changes location, you can alter its appearance so that its movements appear natural for the image. For example, if you create an image of a creature and move it, you can alter the image so that it appears to be walking. Similarly, you can cause the illusion to make different sounds at different times, even making it carry on a conversation, for example.

Physical interaction with the image reveals it to be an illusion, for things can pass through it. A creature that takes a Study action to examine the image can determine that it is an illusion with a successful [[/check ability=int skill=inv dc=@attributes.spell.dc]] check against your spell save DC. If a creature discerns the illusion for what it is, the creature can see through the image, and its other sensory qualities become faint to the creature.

Using a Higher-Level Spell Slot. The spell lasts until dispelled, without requiring Concentration, if cast with a level 4+ spell slot.

The wraith can move through other creatures and objects as if they were difficult terrain.

It takes 5 (1d10) force damage if it ends its turn inside an object.

The wraith can move through other creatures and objects as if they were difficult terrain.

Melee Weapon Attack: +7 to hit, 5 ft., one creature. Hit: 17 (3d8 + 4) force damage.

If the target is a spellcaster, they can choose to spend a spell slot of mitigate some or all of this attack's damage. The damage done by this attack is reduced by 5 per level of spell slot spent. This does not require an action from the target to do.

The Arcane Wraith attacks with its bare hands which are made of pure arcane force. The target can mitigate this effect if they are a spellcaster.

The Arcane Wraith has advantage on saving throws against spells and other magical effects. The Arcane Wraith is also immune to any spells or spell-like powers which would send it to a different plane than that of the portal it is bound to.

The Arcane Wraith seems especially resistant to magical effects!

Any time the Arcane Wraith successfully resists the effect of a spell via a saving throw, it gains 5 hit points per level of the spell it saved against. If the wraith is at full health when consuming a spell, it instead gains temporary hit points.

The Arcane Wraith absorbs residual magical energy that swirls around it!

The Arcane Wraith is magically bound to the area around the planar gateway it protects. It cannot move more than 100ft from the portal, or move to a point where it would not still see the portal.

If it is forced to move out of sight of the portal it will spend its action and movement moving back to the portal by the most direct route possible.

It always inherently knows the direction of the portal.

The arcane wraith is magically bound to its point of origin.

As a reaction, the Arcane Wraith attempts to unravel magical effects as they are being cast. The caster must be within 30 feet of and visible to the Wraith to do this.

The Arcane Wraith makes an Intelligence ability check with a DC equal to 10 + the spell level (cantrips count as level 1). On a success, the creature's spell fails and has no effect. The Arcane Wraith makes the Intelligence ability check with Advantage when attempting to shatter a Necromancy or Restoration spell.

The Arcane Wraith may use this ability three times per day.

The Arcane Wraith's innate connection to magic allows it to reflexively shatter spells as they are created.

Arcane Wraiths that are hit by necrotic or force damage gain hit points equal to the damage done by the attack, absorbing the energy into themselves instead of taking damage. If the Arcane Wraith is already at maximum hit points they instead gain temporary hit points.
The Arcane Wraith makes two Arcane Strike attacks.

description.value: Wizard

Your experience in enforcing the law, and dealing with lawbreakers, gives you a feel for local laws and criminals. You can easily find the local outpost of the watch or a similar organization, and just as easily pick out the dens of criminal activity in a community, although you’re more likely to be welcome in the former locations rather than the latter.

You hurl a mote of fire at a creature or object within range. Make a ranged spell attack against the target. On a hit, the target takes 1d10 fire damage. A flammable object hit by this spell ignites if it isn't being worn or carried.

This spell's damage increases by 1d10 when you reach 5th level (2d10), 11th level (3d10), and 17th level (4d10).
This spell allows you to move at an incredible pace. When you cast this spell, and then as a bonus action on each of your turns until the spell ends, you can take the Dash action.
You touch a creature. The target's speed increases by 10 feet until the spell ends.

You make yourself—including your clothing, armor, weapons, and other belongings on your person—look different until the spell ends or until you use your action to dismiss it. You can seem 1 foot shorter or taller and can appear thin, fat, or in between. You can't change your body type, so you must adopt a form that has the same basic arrangement of limbs. Otherwise, the extent of the illusion is up to you.

The changes wrought by this spell fail to hold up to physical inspection. For example, if you use this spell to add a hat to your outfit, objects pass through the hat, and anyone who touches it would feel nothing or would feel your head and hair. If you use this spell to appear thinner than you are, the hand of someone who reaches out to touch you would bump into you while it was seemingly still in midair.

To discern that you are disguised, a creature can use its action to inspect your appearance and must succeed on an Intelligence (Investigation) check against your spell save DC.

Beginning at 2nd level, you can create pockets of relative safety within the effects of your evocation spells. When you cast an evocation spell that affects other creatures that you can see, you can choose a number of them equal to 1 + the spell's level. The chosen creatures automatically succeed on their saving throws against the spell, and they take no damage if they would normally take half damage on a successful save.
Beginning when you select this school at 2nd level, the gold and time you must spend to copy an evocation spell into your spellbook is halved.

A punch, kick, head-butt, or similar forceful blow (none of which count as weapons). On a hit, an unarmed strike deals bludgeoning damage equal to 1 + your Strength modifier. You are proficient with your unarmed strikes.

A cloth or leather pouch can hold up to 20 sling bullets or 50 blowgun needles, among other things. A compartmentalized pouch for holding spell components is called a component pouch. A pouch can hold up to ⅕ cubic foot or 6 pounds of gear.

These metal restraints can bind a Small or Medium creature. Escaping the manacles requires a successful DC 20 Dexterity check. Breaking them requires a successful DC 20 Strength check. Each set of manacles comes with one key. Without the key, a creature proficient with thieves' tools can pick the manacles' lock with a successful DC 15 Dexterity check. Manacles have 15 hit points.

It's hard to make generalizations about humans, but your human character has these traits.

Ability Score Increase. Your ability scores each increase by 1.

Age. Humans reach adulthood in their late teens and live less than a century.

Alignment. Humans tend toward no particular alignment. The best and the worst are found among them.

Size. Humans vary widely in height and build, from barely 5 feet to well over 6 feet tall. Regardless of your position in that range, your size is Medium.

Speed. Your base walking speed is 30 feet.

Languages. You can speak, read, and write Common and one extra language of your choice. Humans typically learn the languages of other peoples they deal with, including obscure dialects. They are fond of sprinkling their speech with words borrowed from other tongues: Orc curses, Elvish musical expressions, Dwarvish military phrases, and so on.

Choose one object weighing 1 to 5 pounds within range that isn't being worn or carried. The object flies in a straight line up to 90 feet in a direction you choose before falling to the ground, stopping early if it impacts against a solid surface. If the object would strike a creature, that creature must make a Dexterity saving throw. On a failed save, the object strikes the target and stops moving. When the object strikes something, the object and what it strikes each take [[/r 3d8]] bludgeoning damage.

At Higher Levels.

When you cast this spell using a spell slot of 2nd level or higher, the maximum weight of objects that you can target with this spell increases by 5 pounds, and the damage increases by [[/r 1d8]], for each slot level above 1st.

You hurl a 4-inch-diameter sphere of energy at a creature that you can see within range. You choose acid, cold, fire, lightning, poison, or thunder for the type of orb you create, and then make a ranged spell attack against the target. If the attack hits, the creature takes [[/r 3d8]] damage of the type you chose.

At Higher Levels.

When you cast this spell using a spell slot of 2nd level or higher, the damage increases by [[/r 1d8]] for each slot level above 1st.

A square yard of silk of average quality and weight. Used for all many of items and clothing.

The finest and most desirable of the common fabrics, silk is also the lightest. Most silks will weigh between 2 and 4 ounces per square yard. The heavier the silk, the higher the quality, more durable, and more opaque in color it is.

A square yard of linen of average quality and weight. Used for all many of items and clothing.

Longer lasting than cotton, its durability and breathability make it particularly valued in warm climtes.

Different types of linen do exist, with lighter weaves starting at 6 ounces per square yard, and the rest going up to 15 ounces.

You focus your study on magic that creates powerful elemental effects such as bitter cold, searing flame, rolling thunder, crackling lightning, and burning acid. Some evokers find employment in military forces, serving as artillery to blast enemy armies from afar. Others use their spectacular power to protect the weak, while some seek their own gain as bandits, adventurers, or aspiring tyrants.

You have scribed a set of arcane formulas in your spellbook that you can use to formulate a cantrip in your mind. Whenever you finish a long rest and consult those formulas in your spellbook, you can replace one wizard cantrip you know with another cantrip from the wizard spell list.

A sudden loud ringing noise, painfully intense, erupts from a point of your choice within range. Each creature in a 10-foot-radius sphere centered on that point must make a Constitution saving throw. A creature takes [[/damage 3d8 type=thunder]] damage on a failed save, or half as much damage on a successful one. A creature made of inorganic material such as stone, crystal, or metal has disadvantage on this saving throw.

A nonmagical object that isn't being worn or carried also takes the damage if it's in the spell's area.

At Higher Levels.

When you cast this spell using a spell slot of 3rd level or higher, the damage increases by [[/damage 1d8]] for each slot level above 2nd.

When you take nonmagical bludgeoning, piercing, or slashing damage, you can use your reaction to momentarily encase yourself in a watery shell, reducing the damage taken by [[/r 1d6]].

At Higher Levels.

This spell's protection increases by [[/r 1d6]] when you reach certain levels: 5th level ([[/r 2d6]]), 11th level ([[/r 3d6]]), and 17th level ([[/r 4d6]]).

A bright streak flashes from your pointing finger to a point you choose within range and then blossoms with a low roar into an explosion of flame. Each creature in a 20-foot-radius sphere centered on that point must make a Dexterity saving throw. A target takes [[/damage 8d6 type=fire]] damage on a failed save, or half as much damage on a successful one.

The fire spreads around corners. It ignites flammable objects in the area that aren't being worn or carried.

At Higher Levels.

When you cast this spell using a spell slot of 4th level or higher, the damage increases by [[/damage 1d6]] for each slot level above 3rd.

You choose nonmagical flame that you can see within range and that fits within a 5-foot cube. You affect it in one of the following ways:

  • You instantaneously expand the flame 5 feet in one direction, provided that wood or other fuel is present in the new location.
  • You instantaneously extinguish the flames within the cube.
  • You double or halve the area of bright light and dim light cast by the flame, change its color, or both. The change lasts for 1 hour.
  • You cause simple shapes—such as the vague form of a creature, an inanimate object, or a location—to appear within the flames and animate as you like. The shapes last for 1 hour.

If you cast this spell multiple times, you can have up to three non-instantaneous effects created by it active at a time, and you can dismiss such an effect as an action.
Harvesting valuable materials from corpses.
Looting valuables from corpses.
A Robe has vocational or ceremonial significance. Some events and locations admit only people wearing a Robe bearing certain colors or symbols.

An arcane focus is a special item—an orb, a crystal, a rod, a specially constructed staff, a wand-like length of wood, or some similar item—designed to channel the power of arcane spells. A sorcerer, warlock, or wizard can use such an item as a spellcasting focus.

Multiple variations of this item exist, as listed below:

  • @item[Orb|phb]
  • @item[Rod|phb]
  • @item[Staff|phb]
  • @item[Wand|phb]
Essential for wizards, a spellbook is a leather-bound tome with 100 blank vellum pages suitable for recording spells.

You freeze a 5-foot cube of water that you can see within range. Any creatures in the water must succeed on a Dexterity saving throw or become &Reference[condition=restrained]. A &Reference[condition=restrained] creature can use its action to make a Strength check against your spell save DC, breaking the ice around it and freeing itself on a success.

At Higher Levels. When you cast this spell using a spell slot of 2nd level or higher, the size of the cube increases by 5 feet for each slot level above 1st.

This spell allows you to move like water. When you cast this spell, and then as a bonus action on each of your turns until the spell ends, you can propel yourself up to 20 feet in a straight line. If this moves you into another creature's space for the first time on a turn, that creature must succeed on a Strength saving throw or take [[/damage 2d6 type=bludgeoning]] damage and be knocked &Reference[condition=prone].

At Higher Levels. When you cast the spell using a spell slot of 3rd level or higher, the distance you can propel yourself increases by 5 feet for each slot level above 2nd.

You conjure a small storm cloud made solid by magic, which you leap atop as part of casting the spell and your magic causes it to float and fly. You gain a flying speed of 30 feet for the duration. While you fly in this way, the cloud remains beneath you and can provide half cover. If you fall while flying in this way, the spell ends immediately.

In addition, if you fly at least 20 feet straight toward a target using this flying speed on your turn, you can use your bonus action to slam the target using the cloud.

Make a melee spell attack against the target. On a hit, the target takes [[/damage 2d6 type=thunder]] damage.

When the spell ends, the cloud turns to dust and you fall if you are still aloft, unless you can stop the fall.

This spell is a variant of @spell[Terra Steed]

At Higher Levels. When you cast this spell using a spell slot of 4th level or higher, the flying speed you gain increases by 30 feet for each slot level above 3rd.

You calm yourself and focus for a brief moment as you concentrate on elements of the arcane. Choose one of the following damage types: acid, cold, fire, lightning, or thunder. Until the spell ends, your spell attacks deal an extra [[/r 1d6]] of the chosen damage type on a hit.

You release the magical energy from one of the elements in an explosive burst. You choose a point within range that contains one of the following five elements of your choice: air, earth (which includes soil, metal, or stone), fire, water, or wood. That material releases its elemental energy. Each creature within a 15-foot cone emanating from that point must make a saving throw. The victim takes [[/damage 2d6]] damage on a failed save, or half as much damage on a successful one.

The type of saving throw required and damage inflicted depend on the element, as determined by the following table:

Element Type | Saving Throw | Damage Type

Air | Dexterity | Lightning

Earth | Strength | Acid

Fire | Dexterity | Fire

Water | Constitution |Cold

Wood | Constitution | Poison

In addition to taking damage, each creature that fails its saving throw suffers an additional effect, depending on the element type. These effects are detailed below, along with descriptions of each element's exact effect:

Air. There is a sudden flash of light and peal of thunder as a gust of wind whips up out of nowhere, heavy with static electricity that shocks those nearby. Creatures that fail their save are knocked prone. Objects that aren't being worn or carried become electrified, inflicting [[/damage 1d6 type=lightning]] damage on the next person who touches them within the next minute.

Earth. Clumps of metal and rock spray out, oozing a corrosive substance. Creatures who fail their save are pushed back 10 feet away from the point at the center of the effect, as are objects weighing less than 100 lbs. that aren't being worn or carried.

Fire. The fire shoots out glowing sparks. It ignites flammable objects in the area that aren't being worn or carried, and creatures who fail their save take an additional [[/damage 1d6]] damage at the beginning of their next turn.

Water. Icy water pushes out in a freezing wave that crashes into those nearby. Creatures who fail their save reduce their speed by half until the end of their next turn, and objects weighing less than 100 pounds that aren't being worn or carried are pushed back 15 feet away from the point at the center of the effect.

Wood. The element throws off sharp slivers of the same material as itself, infused with a poisonous sap. Creatures who fail their save cannot take reactions until the end of their next turn. Against objects, this effect inflicts piercing damage instead of poison.

The explosive noise of this spell can be heard up to 100 feet away. The spell does not noticeably affect the structure of any object that is the source of the elemental effect, unless it is an object that is not being worn or carried. If that is the case, the object suffers the same [[/damage 2d6]] damage as a creature that failed its saving throw.

At Higher Levels. When you cast this spell using a 2nd level or higher spell slot, the damage increases by [[/r 1d6]] for each slot level above 1st.

description.value: Your experience in enforcing the law, and dealing with lawbreakers, gives you a feel for local laws and criminals. You can easily find the local outpost of the watch or a similar organization, and just as easily pick out the dens of criminal activity in a community, although you're more likely to be welcome in the former locations rather than the latter.

You have served the community where you grew up, standing as its first line of defense against crime. You aren't a soldier, directing your gaze outward at possible enemies. Instead, your service to your hometown was to help police its populace, protecting the citizenry from lawbreakers and malefactors of every stripe.

You might have been part of the City Watch of Waterdeep, the baton-wielding police force of the City of Splendors, protecting the common folk from thieves and rowdy nobility alike. Or you might have been one of the valiant defenders of Silverymoon, a member of the Silverwatch or even one of the magic-wielding Spellguard.

Perhaps you hail from Neverwinter and have served as one of its Wintershield watchmen, the newly founded branch of guards who vow to keep safe the City of Skilled Hands.

Even if you're not city-born or city-bred, this background can describe your early years as a member of law enforcement. Most settlements of any size have their own constables and police forces, and even smaller communities have sheriffs and bailiffs who stand ready to protect their community.

biography.value:
Bowser — The Dragon-King Who Keeps Getting Up

Bowser is the creature who has defined the Mushroom Kingdom through opposition for longer than most of its current inhabitants have been alive. He is the villain of every story, the kidnapper in every legend, the fire-breathing turtle-dragon-king whose name is used to frighten children and whose actual presence frightens things considerably larger than children. He has fought Mario more times than either of them can accurately count. He has been defeated, imprisoned, exiled, launched into the sun, thrown into lava, dropped from airships, and subjected to indignities that would have destroyed any creature whose defining characteristic was anything other than the absolute, pathological refusal to stay down.

Bowser always gets back up. That's the thing about Bowser that makes him terrifying not as a villain but as a FACT. He doesn't stay defeated. He doesn't learn the lesson that everyone thinks defeat is supposed to teach. He stands up, dusts off whatever substance he was thrown into, returns to his castle, rebuilds whatever army Mario scattered, and starts planning the next attempt. The cycle has repeated for decades. The cycle IS Bowser. Without the cycle, he is a very large koopa with anger management issues and an empty castle.

Understanding what Bowser was—at his peak, before the current crisis reduced him from conqueror to captive to reluctant ally to vampire dinner guest—requires understanding the scale of his ambition and the genuine capability that made that ambition something other than delusion.

Bowser consolidated power in Darkland during the chaos following Princess Peach's assassination in 955 BF. While the Mushroom Kingdom fragmented into civil war factions, Bowser built. He unified the Koopa Troop—a loose confederation of koopa, goomba, and allied species—into a genuine military force through a combination of personal dominance, strategic marriages with subordinate clan leaders, and the kind of charismatic brutality that inspires loyalty in creatures who respect strength above all other qualities. By the time the First Bowser Conflict began in approximately 1005 BF, Darkland was the most organized military power in the region, and Bowser was its undisputed ruler.

The kidnapping obsession is the detail that historical analyses either focus on exclusively or dismiss entirely, and both responses miss the point. Bowser kidnapped Princess Toadstool (and later, during the brief period when "Peach" was used for her successor) repeatedly, obsessively, with a persistence that transcended tactical logic and entered the territory of something that psychologists would have opinions about if anyone ever convinced Bowser to attend a session.

The kidnappings were not rational. Bowser could have conquered Mushroom Kingdom territory through conventional military force at several points during the civil war period when the kingdom's defenses were at their weakest. He chose not to. Instead, he kidnapped princesses, built elaborate castle obstacles, positioned his subordinates in fortresses across eight worlds of territory, and WAITED for Mario to come. The entire invasion infrastructure was designed not to prevent rescue but to make rescue as dramatic as possible.

Waluigi—who has analyzed Bowser with the dedication of someone who has lost to him at every competitive event they've ever entered—believes the kidnappings were not conquest but courtship. Not romantic courtship in the conventional sense, but the courtship of someone who didn't know how to express desire except through control. Bowser wanted Peach (or her successor) the way he wanted everything: absolutely, unilaterally, without the complication of the other person's feelings or the recognition that relationships require consent rather than capture.

This interpretation doesn't excuse the kidnappings. It contextualizes them as the behavior of someone whose emotional development was shaped by a species and culture where taking what you want is the primary social mechanism, where strength determines entitlement, and where the concept of "asking" is foreign enough to require translation. Bowser didn't kidnap princesses because he was evil. He kidnapped princesses because his entire frame of reference for acquiring things he valued was "take them and defend your claim."

The Chaos Heart Crisis of 1025 BF represents the most complicated chapter of Bowser's history. He was one of the forced participants in the wedding that triggered the Chaos Heart's awakening—married to Princess Peach (the successor) against both their wills by Count Bleck. The ceremony was not about their feelings; it was about the conceptual union of opposing forces creating the paradox that empowered the Chaos Heart. Bowser was a tool. The experience of being USED—of having his agency removed and his body deployed as a component in someone else's plan—was transformative in ways that Bowser has never discussed and that observers have never adequately analyzed.

After the Crisis, Bowser's behavior changed in subtle but detectable ways. His invasion attempts became less frequent. His castle defenses became less elaborate. His interaction with Junior—always complicated by absence—acquired a quality that might have been guilt or might have been the recognition that empire-building costs things that can't be rebuilt. He still fought Mario. He still kidnapped (less often). He still roared and breathed fire and broke things. But something underneath the performance had shifted, the way a foundation shifts under a building that still looks solid from outside.

The current crisis has stripped away whatever remained of Bowser's pretensions to empire. He was captured aboard the Vigilance. He was traded between factions like cargo. He was taken captive by Wally (Waluigi's agent) and Bowser still doesn't fully understand the political dimensions of what happened to him. He attended Orangus Cornelius's vampire dinner party in the Shadowfell as a GUEST—not a conqueror, not an invader, a guest who followed etiquette because the alternative was worse. He examined necromancer wands with the curiosity of someone who has stopped pretending that magic beneath his station doesn't interest him.

He fought alongside the party at Raventree Manor. He participated in the Oracle's failed ritual. He has been scattered across dimensions by the Planar Fracture, reformed alliances with people he would have conquered a decade ago, and demonstrated capabilities and qualities that the Bowser of 1005 BF would have considered beneath his dignity. He has punched ghosts with his bare fists because Archie needed time to cast ice spells. He has accepted tactical direction from toads who weigh less than his left arm. He has cooperated.

This is the Bowser who exists now: still enormous, still fire-breathing, still capable of violence that makes architecture regret being built, but tempered by decades of defeat, by the loss of his empire, by the absence from his son, and by the creeping realization that the cycle of kidnapping and rescue and defeat was never going to give him what he actually wanted. What he actually wanted was connection. What he actually wanted was for someone to choose to be near him rather than being forced to be near him. What he actually wanted was something that his entire species and culture had no vocabulary for, and that his own behavior made impossible.

Bowser at his peak was a natural disaster with a crown. Bowser now is something more complicated and more dangerous: a natural disaster that's learning to think.
biography.public: A massive koopa dragon-king whose shell is scarred from decades of defeats he survived through stubbornness alone. He fills every room he enters, breathes fire when he's annoyed, and has recently started cooperating with people he used to try to conquer. This last development worries everyone, including Bowser.

description.value:
Bowser's primary weapons are attached to his body and have been since birth. His claws can rend steel, his fists can shatter stone, and his grip can crush things that were designed to be crush-resistant. He doesn't carry weapons because he IS a weapon—every component of his body optimized through species and personal development for the specific purpose of destroying whatever he's directed toward.

His fighting style is self-taught through decades of combat against the most capable hero the Mushroom Kingdom has ever produced. Mario forced Bowser to improve. Every defeat revealed a weakness that Bowser addressed for the next encounter. Every near-victory showed a strength that Bowser refined. The result is a combat capability that has been honed against the best possible opponent for over thirty-five years—not elegant, not subtle, but devastatingly effective against anything that hasn't been specifically trained to counter Bowser's particular combination of speed, power, and the unsettling creativity of someone who has learned to fight by losing to a genius.

The punching-ghosts incident at Raventree Manor demonstrated something that shouldn't be possible: Bowser physically striking incorporeal entities through sheer force of personality and the particular density of a fist that has been clenched in fury so many times that even spiritual beings recognize it as a threat. Whether this reflects magical contamination from decades of exposure to supernatural events or simply Bowser's refusal to accept that something can't be punched, the effect is the same: his attacks count as magical for purposes of overcoming resistance.
description.chat: Claws that have shredded castle walls and fists that have punched ghosts into acknowledging physical reality. He doesn't need weapons. He is one.

unidentified.name: Natural Weapons
unidentified.description: This creature's natural claws and fists deliver devastating force that somehow affects even incorporeal entities.

description.value:
Bowser's shell is not armor he wears but anatomy he was born with, reinforced through decades of combat that have deposited layers of impact-hardened keratin over the original structure. The shell's spikes are genuine defensive weapons—creatures that grapple Bowser from behind or attempt to mount his shell take 2d6 piercing damage at the start of each of their turns as the spikes dig into whatever flesh is pressing against them.

The shell provides AC 21 (natural armor) and is the primary reason Bowser has survived injuries that would have killed conventional creatures multiple times over. It has absorbed dragon fire, magical explosions, being thrown into stars (this happened at least twice, according to accounts Waluigi considers credible), and the specific kind of architectural collapse that occurs when a structure not designed to contain a Bowser fight is forced to contain one anyway.

The shell also serves as a vehicle. Bowser can withdraw into it and spin, converting himself into a projectile that deals devastating damage to anything in his path. This technique was developed during his fights with Mario and refined through the kind of iterative engineering that occurs when your enemy keeps finding new ways to dodge your fire and you need alternatives.
description.chat: The shell is scarred from every battle he's survived, each mark a defeat that would have killed something less stubborn. The spikes are a reminder that attacking him from behind is also a bad idea.

unidentified.name: Spiked Natural Shell
unidentified.description: A massive spiked shell that provides extraordinary natural armor and serves as both defense and weapon.

description.value:
Bowser withdraws into his shell and launches himself as a spinning projectile, crossing up to 40 feet in a straight line and devastating everything in his path. The technique combines the rotational force of his massive body with the spiked shell's cutting capability, creating a mobile hazard that shreds through obstacles and enemies with equal disregard.

Each creature in Bowser's path must make a DC 21 Dexterity saving throw. On a failure, a creature takes 4d10 + 8 bludgeoning damage plus 2d6 piercing damage from the spikes and is knocked prone. On a success, a creature takes half damage and isn't knocked prone but is pushed 10 feet to either side of Bowser's path. Objects and structures in the path take double damage as the spinning shell grinds through them.

After the spin, Bowser emerges from his shell in the space at the end of his path. He cannot use Shell Spin again until the start of his next turn, as reorienting from the spin requires a moment of recovery. This recovery period—approximately two seconds—is the window Mario learned to exploit during their fights, and it remains Bowser's most consistent vulnerability during combat.
description.chat: The shell spins, spikes blur into a circle of destruction, and everything between Bowser and his destination learns that standing in a dragon-king's path is a structural engineering problem, not a combat one.

unidentified.name: Spinning Shell Charge
unidentified.description: This creature can withdraw into its spiked shell and launch itself as a devastating projectile.

description.value:
Bowser leaps and slams his full weight into the ground, creating shockwaves that radiate outward in a 20-foot radius. The technique exploits the simple physics of dropping something extremely heavy from height—Bowser weighs enough that his landing registers on seismographic equipment from considerable distance. The shockwaves crack stone, shatter glass, and knock anyone who isn't braced off their feet.

Each creature within 20 feet of the impact point must make a DC 21 Strength saving throw. On a failure, a creature takes 3d10 + 8 bludgeoning damage and is knocked prone. On a success, a creature takes half damage and isn't knocked prone. The ground in the affected area becomes difficult terrain as cracks, rubble, and displaced material make footing treacherous.
description.chat: He goes up. He comes down. Everything between 'up' and 'down' ceases to be solid.

unidentified.name: Seismic Slam
unidentified.description: This creature can leap and slam the ground, creating shockwaves that damage and topple everything in a wide radius.

description.value: Bowser's jaws can close with force sufficient to sever limbs and crush armor. His bite attack is typically reserved for enemies who have gotten close enough to grapple or for situations where his claws are occupied. The bite is enhanced by the same biological furnace that produces his fire breath—targets bitten feel residual heat from the furnace's proximity, and the wound often cauterizes partially on infliction.
description.chat: Jaws close with the finality of a drawbridge slamming shut, heat radiating from a mouth that doubles as a furnace.

unidentified.name: Crushing Bite
unidentified.description: A devastating bite attack from jaws that radiate heat.

description.value:
Bowser has been defeated more times than any creature in documented history and has survived every single time. Thrown into lava, launched into stars, crushed by collapsing castles, dropped from airships at terminal velocity—he has experienced fatal events that would create multiple sequential deaths for conventional creatures and has emerged from each one angry, slightly singed, and ready for the next round.

Three times per long rest, when Bowser is reduced to 0 hit points but not killed outright, he drops to 1 hit point instead. Each use of this ability produces a visible effect: his eyes burn brighter, his shell's spikes lengthen slightly, and the ground under his feet cracks from the physical manifestation of his refusal to accept defeat. He doesn't recover through healing or resilience. He recovers through STUBBORNNESS—the fundamental quality that defines him more than fire breath or strength or the crown he hasn't worn in months.

After using all three instances in a single combat, Bowser can be brought to 0 hit points normally. But by the time an enemy has put him down four times, the environment around the fight has typically been so thoroughly destroyed that continuing the engagement becomes an architectural concern rather than a tactical one.
description.chat: He falls. He gets up. He falls again. He gets up again. At some point the enemy has to decide whether killing Bowser is physically possible or just theoretically interesting.

description.value:
Bowser learns from every fight. This is the quality that makes him genuinely dangerous rather than merely powerful—a creature that simply hits hard can be countered, but a creature that adapts its approach based on what it learns from being countered is a problem that gets harder with each engagement.

After the first round of combat, Bowser gains advantage on attack rolls against any creature that has successfully hit him, as he's catalogued their attack patterns and adjusted his defense and positioning accordingly. After the second round, he gains resistance to the most common damage type he's received, as his body and tactics adapt to prioritize defense against demonstrated threats. After the third round, he can use a reaction to impose disadvantage on one attack roll against him per round, as his understanding of the enemy's patterns becomes comprehensive enough to predict and counter specific attacks.

This adaptation resets between combats as different opponents require different assessments. But the ABILITY to adapt doesn't reset—thirty-five years of fighting the most capable hero in the kingdom have built neural pathways for combat learning that other creatures simply don't possess.
description.chat: Hit him once and he learns your timing. Hit him twice and he learns your patterns. Hit him three times and he knows exactly what you're going to do before you do it.

description.value: Three times per day, when Bowser fails a saving throw, he can choose to succeed instead. He has been hit with everything—petrification, banishment, mind control, temporal displacement, the Chaos Heart's reality-warping effects—and he has shrugged off all of it through the same mechanism that keeps him alive: the fundamental, bone-deep refusal to be stopped by anything he hasn't decided to stop for.
description.chat: The effect hits. Bowser doesn't care. He has survived worse. He has survived EVERYTHING.

description.value:
Bowser can take 3 legendary actions, choosing from the options below. Only one legendary action can be used at a time and only at the end of another creature's turn.

Claw Swipe (1 action): Bowser makes one claw attack against a creature within reach.

Roar (1 action): Bowser roars with force that shakes the room. Each creature within 30 feet that can hear him must succeed on a DC 18 Wisdom saving throw or be frightened until the end of its next turn. Creatures that have fought Bowser before have disadvantage on this save, having learned that the roar usually precedes something worse.

Fire Snap (2 actions): Bowser breathes a quick burst of fire at a single target within 30 feet. The target must make a DC 20 Dexterity saving throw, taking 6d6 fire damage on a failure or half on a success.

Unstoppable Advance (2 actions): Bowser moves up to his speed. This movement doesn't provoke opportunity attacks, and any creature in his path must succeed on a DC 21 Strength saving throw or be pushed 10 feet ahead of him and knocked prone. Objects in his path take 4d10 bludgeoning damage.

Giga Bowser Rage (3 actions, 1/day): Bowser draws on reserves of fury that temporarily increase his size from Large to Huge for 1 round. His reach increases to 15 feet, his damage dice increase by one size category, and he gains 30 temporary hit points. After this round ends, he returns to Large size and cannot use legendary actions until the start of his next turn.
description.chat: Between other creatures' heartbeats, Bowser acts—clawing, roaring, burning, advancing, growing. The dragon-king doesn't wait for his turn because waiting was never part of his personality.

description.value:
Bowser is not the creature he was in 1005 BF. Decades of defeat, the Chaos Heart Crisis, the loss of his empire, separation from his son, and the current crisis's forced alliances have produced changes that the old Bowser would have considered weakness and that the current Bowser is slowly, reluctantly beginning to recognize as growth.

He cooperates with people he would have conquered. He follows tactical direction from creatures he could crush with one hand. He attended a vampire dinner party and used silverware instead of his claws. He punched ghosts to buy time for a wizard he doesn't like because the situation required teamwork rather than dominance. Each of these moments represents a compromise with the version of himself that spent decades trying to take everything by force and learning, repeatedly, that force alone doesn't work.

This change is not complete. Bowser still defaults to aggression when stressed. He still thinks in terms of conquest and control. He still believes, on some level, that being the strongest should entitle him to whatever he wants. But the defaults are being overridden more frequently by something that looks suspiciously like judgment, and the beliefs are being contradicted by experiences that keep proving them wrong.

The party interacts with a Bowser in transition—not the villain they might expect from legends, not the ally they might want, but something in between that is figuring out what it is in real time. He will fight alongside them if the situation demands it. He will argue with them about tactics, objectives, and whether punching something is the correct response to a problem (his position: always yes). He will occasionally do something selfless and then immediately deny that selflessness was involved. And he will, in moments of quiet honesty, wonder what kind of king he would have been if he'd learned these lessons before he lost everything.
description.chat: The dragon-king who kidnapped princesses is learning to cooperate with toads. It's not comfortable. It's not natural. But it might be the thing that finally makes him the king he always wanted to be.

description.value:
Bowser allegedly owes Wario 50,000 gold pieces for "storage fees" related to keeping some of Bowser's treasure safe during a battle. The actual situation: Wario stole half of Bowser's treasure and is now charging Bowser to return the other half. Bowser is aware that this arrangement is extortion. Bowser has not killed Wario over it because—and this surprises everyone who knows both parties—Bowser finds Wario's audacity entertaining in a way that genuine enemies never manage. There is a grudging respect between them that neither would call friendship and both would deny if asked.

The debt appears in Wario's ledger, in Bowser's grudging acknowledgment, and in the bizarre political reality that these two creatures—one a former dragon-king, one a con artist with a coin press—have a business relationship that has survived longer than most of the factions currently fighting over the Mushroom Kingdom's future.
description.chat: Fifty thousand gold. For storing treasure he stole. And Bowser hasn't killed him for it. This might be the most confusing relationship in the entire crisis.

unidentified.name: Outstanding Debt Document
unidentified.description: A debt record between this creature and a notorious con artist, representing an extortion arrangement that both parties have somehow maintained through mutual grudging respect.

description.value:
Bowser's fire breath is the most iconic destructive capability in the Mushroom Kingdom, a weapon that has destroyed castles, routed armies, and—according to Waluigi's research—once ignited an entire lake through means that physicists still debate. The fire originates from a biological furnace unique to koopa dragon-kings, fueled by a diet that includes metals, minerals, and whatever else Bowser feels like eating. The flame temperature exceeds what organic biology should produce, suggesting either magical enhancement, evolutionary anomaly, or simple refusal to conform to the laws of thermodynamics.

Bowser exhales fire in a 60-foot cone. Each creature in the cone must make a DC 20 Dexterity saving throw, taking 12d6 fire damage on a failure or half on a success. The fire ignites flammable objects in the area that aren't being worn or carried. The breath weapon recharges on a roll of 5-6 on a d6 at the start of Bowser's turn.

The fire breath's destructive potential has been a strategic factor in every conflict Bowser has participated in. Castles are built to resist it. Armies train formations to scatter when the breath begins charging. And Mario learned, very early in their rivalry, that the three seconds between the inhale and the exhale are the most important seconds in any fight against Bowser—if you're not out of the cone by then, you're not getting out.
description.chat: He inhales. The air around him superheats. And then fire erupts in a torrent that turns architectural ambition into archaeology.

description.value: Bowser makes three attacks: two claw strikes and one bite, or two claw strikes and one Ground Pound, or one Shell Spin (which replaces his entire action). He can substitute his Fire Breath for any two attacks if it's available.
description.chat: Claws, teeth, weight, fire—every part of him is a weapon and they all arrive in the same round.

description.value:
Bowser has a son who is currently building a vehicle in the deepest workshop of Koopa Castle to come find him. Bowser doesn't know this. He doesn't know that Junior is worried, that Kamek is consolidating power over the Koopa Troop remnants, or that his son's mythology about an invincible father is crumbling under the weight of reality. He knows only that Junior exists, that Junior needs him, and that he's currently in a dimension where reaching Junior is impossible.

The separation from Junior affects Bowser's behavior in ways he doesn't acknowledge and barely understands. He becomes more reckless in combat when he feels purposeless—as though proving his strength to absent witnesses might somehow communicate across dimensions. He becomes more protective of small creatures when Junior's absence weighs heavily, transferring parental instinct to whatever vulnerable beings are nearby. And he becomes more cooperative with the party when he recognizes that cooperation might be the path back to his son, because returning to Junior is the one objective that overrides his pride, his aggression, and his stubborn independence.

If the party uses Junior as leverage—threatening his safety or promising to facilitate reunion—Bowser's response depends on whether the approach feels genuine. Genuine concern for Junior produces cooperation that nothing else can achieve. Manipulation using Junior produces violence that nothing can survive.
description.chat: Somewhere, his son is building something to come find him. Bowser doesn't know this. But something in his chest that isn't fire aches when he's quiet long enough to feel it.

description.value: The boneless needn't spend extra movement to move a creature it is grappling.

biography.value:

Whether this reflects magical contamination from decades of exposure to supernatural events or simply Bowser's refusal to accept that something can't be punched, the effect is the same: his attacks count as magical for purposes of overcoming resistance.
description.chat: Claws that have shredded castle walls and fists that have punched ghosts into acknowledging physical reality. He doesn't need weapons. He is one.

unidentified.name: Natural Weapons
unidentified.description: This creature's natural claws and fists deliver devastating force that somehow affects even incorporeal entities.

description.value:
Bowser's shell is not armor he wears but anatomy he was born with, reinforced through decades of combat that have deposited layers of impact-hardened keratin over the original structure. The shell's spikes are genuine defensive weapons—creatures that grapple Bowser from behind or attempt to mount his shell take 2d6 piercing damage at the start of each of their turns as the spikes dig into whatever flesh is pressing against them.

The shell provides AC 21 (natural armor) and is the primary reason Bowser has survived injuries that would have killed conventional creatures multiple times over. It has absorbed dragon fire, magical explosions, being thrown into stars (this happened at least twice, according to accounts Waluigi considers credible), and the specific kind of architectural collapse that occurs when a structure not designed to contain a Bowser fight is forced to contain one anyway.

The shell also serves as a vehicle. Bowser can withdraw into it and spin, converting himself into a projectile that deals devastating damage to anything in his path. This technique was developed during his fights with Mario and refined through the kind of iterative engineering that occurs when your enemy keeps finding new ways to dodge your fire and you need alternatives.
description.chat: The shell is scarred from every battle he's survived, each mark a defeat that would have killed something less stubborn. The spikes are a reminder that attacking him from behind is also a bad idea.

unidentified.name: Spiked Natural Shell
unidentified.description: A massive spiked shell that provides extraordinary natural armor and serves as both defense and weapon.

description.value:
Bowser withdraws into his shell and launches himself as a spinning projectile, crossing up to 40 feet in a straight line and devastating everything in his path. The technique combines the rotational force of his massive body with the spiked shell's cutting capability, creating a mobile hazard that shreds through obstacles and enemies with equal disregard.

Each creature in Bowser's path must make a DC 21 Dexterity saving throw. On a failure, a creature takes 4d10 + 8 bludgeoning damage plus 2d6 piercing damage from the spikes and is knocked prone. On a success, a creature takes half damage and isn't knocked prone but is pushed 10 feet to either side of Bowser's path. Objects and structures in the path take double damage as the spinning shell grinds through them.

After the spin, Bowser emerges from his shell in the space at the end of his path. He cannot use Shell Spin again until the start of his next turn, as reorienting from the spin requires a moment of recovery. This recovery period—approximately two seconds—is the window Mario learned to exploit during their fights, and it remains Bowser's most consistent vulnerability during combat.
description.chat: The shell spins, spikes blur into a circle of destruction, and everything between Bowser and his destination learns that standing in a dragon-king's path is a structural engineering problem, not a combat one.

unidentified.name: Spinning Shell Charge
unidentified.description: This creature can withdraw into its spiked shell and launch itself as a devastating projectile.

description.value:
Bowser leaps and slams his full weight into the ground, creating shockwaves that radiate outward in a 20-foot radius. The technique exploits the simple physics of dropping something extremely heavy from height—Bowser weighs enough that his landing registers on seismographic equipment from considerable distance. The shockwaves crack stone, shatter glass, and knock anyone who isn't braced off their feet.

Each creature within 20 feet of the impact point must make a DC 21 Strength saving throw. On a failure, a creature takes 3d10 + 8 bludgeoning damage and is knocked prone. On a success, a creature takes half damage and isn't knocked prone. The ground in the affected area becomes difficult terrain as cracks, rubble, and displaced material make footing treacherous.
description.chat: He goes up. He comes down. Everything between 'up' and 'down' ceases to be solid.

unidentified.name: Seismic Slam
unidentified.description: This creature can leap and slam the ground, creating shockwaves that damage and topple everything in a wide radius.

description.value: Bowser's jaws can close with force sufficient to sever limbs and crush armor. His bite attack is typically reserved for enemies who have gotten close enough to grapple or for situations where his claws are occupied. The bite is enhanced by the same biological furnace that produces his fire breath—targets bitten feel residual heat from the furnace's proximity, and the wound often cauterizes partially on infliction.
description.chat: Jaws close with the finality of a drawbridge slamming shut, heat radiating from a mouth that doubles as a furnace.

unidentified.name: Crushing Bite
unidentified.description: A devastating bite attack from jaws that radiate heat.

description.value:
Bowser has been defeated more times than any creature in documented history and has survived every single time. Thrown into lava, launched into stars, crushed by collapsing castles, dropped from airships at terminal velocity—he has experienced fatal events that would create multiple sequential deaths for conventional creatures and has emerged from each one angry, slightly singed, and ready for the next round.

Three times per long rest, when Bowser is reduced to 0 hit points but not killed outright, he drops to 1 hit point instead. Each use of this ability produces a visible effect: his eyes burn brighter, his shell's spikes lengthen slightly, and the ground under his feet cracks from the physical manifestation of his refusal to accept defeat. He doesn't recover through healing or resilience. He recovers through STUBBORNNESS—the fundamental quality that defines him more than fire breath or strength or the crown he hasn't worn in months.

After using all three instances in a single combat, Bowser can be brought to 0 hit points normally. But by the time an enemy has put him down four times, the environment around the fight has typically been so thoroughly destroyed that continuing the engagement becomes an architectural concern rather than a tactical one.
description.chat: He falls. He gets up. He falls again. He gets up again. At some point the enemy has to decide whether killing Bowser is physically possible or just theoretically interesting.

description.value:
Bowser learns from every fight. This is the quality that makes him genuinely dangerous rather than merely powerful—a creature that simply hits hard can be countered, but a creature that adapts its approach based on what it learns from being countered is a problem that gets harder with each engagement.

After the first round of combat, Bowser gains advantage on attack rolls against any creature that has successfully hit him, as he's catalogued their attack patterns and adjusted his defense and positioning accordingly. After the second round, he gains resistance to the most common damage type he's received, as his body and tactics adapt to prioritize defense against demonstrated threats. After the third round, he can use a reaction to impose disadvantage on one attack roll against him per round, as his understanding of the enemy's patterns becomes comprehensive enough to predict and counter specific attacks.

This adaptation resets between combats as different opponents require different assessments. But the ABILITY to adapt doesn't reset—thirty-five years of fighting the most capable hero in the kingdom have built neural pathways for combat learning that other creatures simply don't possess.
description.chat: Hit him once and he learns your timing. Hit him twice and he learns your patterns. Hit him three times and he knows exactly what you're going to do before you do it.

description.value: Three times per day, when Bowser fails a saving throw, he can choose to succeed instead. He has been hit with everything—petrification, banishment, mind control, temporal displacement, the Chaos Heart's reality-warping effects—and he has shrugged off all of it through the same mechanism that keeps him alive: the fundamental, bone-deep refusal to be stopped by anything he hasn't decided to stop for.
description.chat: The effect hits. Bowser doesn't care. He has survived worse. He has survived EVERYTHING.

description.value:
Bowser can take 3 legendary actions, choosing from the options below. Only one legendary action can be used at a time and only at the end of another creature's turn.

Claw Swipe (1 action): Bowser makes one claw attack against a creature within reach.

Roar (1 action): Bowser roars with force that shakes the room. Each creature within 30 feet that can hear him must succeed on a DC 18 Wisdom saving throw or be frightened until the end of its next turn. Creatures that have fought Bowser before have disadvantage on this save, having learned that the roar usually precedes something worse.

Fire Snap (2 actions): Bowser breathes a quick burst of fire at a single target within 30 feet. The target must make a DC 20 Dexterity saving throw, taking 6d6 fire damage on a failure or half on a success.

Unstoppable Advance (2 actions): Bowser moves up to his speed. This movement doesn't provoke opportunity attacks, and any creature in his path must succeed on a DC 21 Strength saving throw or be pushed 10 feet ahead of him and knocked prone. Objects in his path take 4d10 bludgeoning damage.

Giga Bowser Rage (3 actions, 1/day): Bowser draws on reserves of fury that temporarily increase his size from Large to Huge for 1 round. His reach increases to 15 feet, his damage dice increase by one size category, and he gains 30 temporary hit points. After this round ends, he returns to Large size and cannot use legendary actions until the start of his next turn.
description.chat: Between other creatures' heartbeats, Bowser acts—clawing, roaring, burning, advancing, growing. The dragon-king doesn't wait for his turn because waiting was never part of his personality.

description.value:
Bowser is not the creature he was in 1005 BF. Decades of defeat, the Chaos Heart Crisis, the loss of his empire, separation from his son, and the current crisis's forced alliances have produced changes that the old Bowser would have considered weakness and that the current Bowser is slowly, reluctantly beginning to recognize as growth.

He cooperates with people he would have conquered. He follows tactical direction from creatures he could crush with one hand. He attended a vampire dinner party and used silverware instead of his claws. He punched ghosts to buy time for a wizard he doesn't like because the situation required teamwork rather than dominance. Each of these moments represents a compromise with the version of himself that spent decades trying to take everything by force and learning, repeatedly, that force alone doesn't work.

This change is not complete. Bowser still defaults to aggression when stressed. He still thinks in terms of conquest and control. He still believes, on some level, that being the strongest should entitle him to whatever he wants. But the defaults are being overridden more frequently by something that looks suspiciously like judgment, and the beliefs are being contradicted by experiences that keep proving them wrong.

The party interacts with a Bowser in transition—not the villain they might expect from legends, not the ally they might want, but something in between that is figuring out what it is in real time. He will fight alongside them if the situation demands it. He will argue with them about tactics, objectives, and whether punching something is the correct response to a problem (his position: always yes). He will occasionally do something selfless and then immediately deny that selflessness was involved. And he will, in moments of quiet honesty, wonder what kind of king he would have been if he'd learned these lessons before he lost everything.
description.chat: The dragon-king who kidnapped princesses is learning to cooperate with toads. It's not comfortable. It's not natural. But it might be the thing that finally makes him the king he always wanted to be.

description.value:
Bowser allegedly owes Wario 50,000 gold pieces for "storage fees" related to keeping some of Bowser's treasure safe during a battle. The actual situation: Wario stole half of Bowser's treasure and is now charging Bowser to return the other half. Bowser is aware that this arrangement is extortion. Bowser has not killed Wario over it because—and this surprises everyone who knows both parties—Bowser finds Wario's audacity entertaining in a way that genuine enemies never manage. There is a grudging respect between them that neither would call friendship and both would deny if asked.

The debt appears in Wario's ledger, in Bowser's grudging acknowledgment, and in the bizarre political reality that these two creatures—one a former dragon-king, one a con artist with a coin press—have a business relationship that has survived longer than most of the factions currently fighting over the Mushroom Kingdom's future.
description.chat: Fifty thousand gold. For storing treasure he stole. And Bowser hasn't killed him for it. This might be the most confusing relationship in the entire crisis.

unidentified.name: Outstanding Debt Document
unidentified.description: A debt record between this creature and a notorious con artist, representing an extortion arrangement that both parties have somehow maintained through mutual grudging respect.

description.value:
Bowser's fire breath is the most iconic destructive capability in the Mushroom Kingdom, a weapon that has destroyed castles, routed armies, and—according to Waluigi's research—once ignited an entire lake through means that physicists still debate. The fire originates from a biological furnace unique to koopa dragon-kings, fueled by a diet that includes metals, minerals, and whatever else Bowser feels like eating. The flame temperature exceeds what organic biology should produce, suggesting either magical enhancement, evolutionary anomaly, or simple refusal to conform to the laws of thermodynamics.

Bowser exhales fire in a 60-foot cone. Each creature in the cone must make a DC 20 Dexterity saving throw, taking 12d6 fire damage on a failure or half on a success. The fire ignites flammable objects in the area that aren't being worn or carried. The breath weapon recharges on a roll of 5-6 on a d6 at the start of Bowser's turn.

The fire breath's destructive potential has been a strategic factor in every conflict Bowser has participated in. Castles are built to resist it. Armies train formations to scatter when the breath begins charging. And Mario learned, very early in their rivalry, that the three seconds between the inhale and the exhale are the most important seconds in any fight against Bowser—if you're not out of the cone by then, you're not getting out.
description.chat: He inhales. The air around him superheats. And then fire erupts in a torrent that turns architectural ambition into archaeology.

description.value: Bowser makes three attacks: two claw strikes and one bite, or two claw strikes and one Ground Pound, or one Shell Spin (which replaces his entire action). He can substitute his Fire Breath for any two attacks if it's available.
description.chat: Claws, teeth, weight, fire—every part of him is a weapon and they all arrive in the same round.

description.value:
Bowser has a son who is currently building a vehicle in the deepest workshop of Koopa Castle to come find him. Bowser doesn't know this. He doesn't know that Junior is worried, that Kamek is consolidating power over the Koopa Troop remnants, or that his son's mythology about an invincible father is crumbling under the weight of reality. He knows only that Junior exists, that Junior needs him, and that he's currently in a dimension where reaching Junior is impossible.

The separation from Junior affects Bowser's behavior in ways he doesn't acknowledge and barely understands. He becomes more reckless in combat when he feels purposeless—as though proving his strength to absent witnesses might somehow communicate across dimensions. He becomes more protective of small creatures when Junior's absence weighs heavily, transferring parental instinct to whatever vulnerable beings are nearby. And he becomes more cooperative with the party when he recognizes that cooperation might be the path back to his son, because returning to Junior is the one objective that overrides his pride, his aggression, and his stubborn independence.

If the party uses Junior as leverage—threatening his safety or promising to facilitate reunion—Bowser's response depends on whether the approach feels genuine. Genuine concern for Junior produces cooperation that nothing else can achieve. Manipulation using Junior produces violence that nothing can survive.
description.chat: Somewhere, his son is building something to come find him. Bowser doesn't know this. But something in his chest that isn't fire aches when he's quiet long enough to feel it.

description.value: The boneless needn't spend extra movement to move a creature it is grappling.
The Bramblefly makes two melee attacks: one with its bite and one with its stinger.

Melee Weapon Attack: +7 to hit, 10 ft., one creature. Hit: 11 (2d6 + 4) piercing damage.

The Bramblefly attacks with its Bite.

Melee Weapon Attack: +7 to hit, 10 ft., one creature. Hit: 10 (1d12 + 4) piercing damage.

The target must make a DC 14 Constitution saving throw, taking 9 (3d6) poison damage on a failed save, or half as much damage on a successful one.

The Bramblefly attacks with its Stinger. The target must make a Constitution saving throw.

Ranged Weapon Attack: +7 to hit, range 100/200 ft., one target. Hit: 8 (1d8 + 4) piercing damage. 

The target must make a DC 14 Constitution saving throw, taking 9 (3d6) poison damage on a failed save, or half as much damage on a successful one.

The Bramblefly launches a barrage of Tail Spikes.
The Bramblefly doesn't provoke opportunity attacks when it flies out of an enemy's reach.

While the Bramblefly is flying or hovering it has advantage on Dexterity saving throws against effects that it can see, such as traps and spells. To gain this benefit, it can't be blinded, incapacitated.

Additionally, while flying, if the Bramblefly is subjected to an effect that allows it to make a Dexterity saving throw to take only half damage, it instead takes no damage if it succeeds on the saving throw, and only half damage if it fails.

If the Bramblefly moves at least 20 feet in a straight line it can use its action to grab a target and snatch them off their feet. The targeted creature must make a successful DC 15 Dexterity Saving throw to avoid being grabbed.

On failure the creature is grappled and the Bramblefly which flies straight up with the remainder of its movement. At the end of its movement it makes a Bite attack against the grappled victim, then releases them, causing them to fall.

The Bramblefly rushes a target from the air, snatching them off their feet! While in the air it bites and then drops them.

description.value: This armor consists of a fitted metal chest piece worn with supple leather. Although it leaves the legs and arms relatively unprotected, this armor provides good protection for the wearer's vital organs while leaving the wearer relatively unencumbered.

Melee Weapon Attack: +3 to hit, 5 ft., one target. Hit: 5 (1d8 + 1) piercing damage.

 

Byscilla attacks with her Rapier.
You touch a willing creature who isn't wearing armor. Until the spell ends, the target's base AC becomes 13 plus its Dexterity modifier. The spell ends early if the target dons armor.

effects.name: Mage Armor
effects.description: The target's base AC becomes 13 + its Dexterity modifier.

description.value:
You create three glowing darts of magical force. Each dart strikes a creature of your choice that you can see within range. A dart deals 1d4 + 1 Force damage to its target. The darts all strike simultaneously, and you can direct them to hit one creature or several.

Using a Higher-Level Spell Slot. The spell creates one more dart for each spell slot level above 1.

[[2 + @item.level]]{Level [[lookup @item.level]] darts}

You touch one Large or smaller object that isn't being worn or carried by someone else. Until the spell ends, the object sheds Bright Light in a 20-foot radius and Dim Light for an additional 20 feet. The light can be colored as you like.

Covering the object with something opaque blocks the light. The spell ends if you cast it again.

A spectral, floating hand appears at a point you choose within range. The hand lasts for the duration. The hand vanishes if it is ever more than 30 feet away from you or if you cast this spell again.

When you cast the spell, you can use the hand to manipulate an object, open an unlocked door or container, stow or retrieve an item from an open container, or pour the contents out of a vial.

As a Magic action on your later turns, you can control the hand thus again. As part of that action, you can move the hand up to 30 feet.

The hand can't attack, activate magic items, or carry more than 10 pounds.

Your body becomes blurred. For the duration, any creature has Disadvantage on attack rolls against you. An attacker is immune to this effect if it perceives you with &Reference[blindsight] or &Reference[truesight].

effects.name: Blurred
effects.description: For the duration, any creature has Disadvantage on attack rolls against you. An attacker is immune to this effect if it perceives you with Blindsight or Truesight.

description.value:
For the duration, you understand the literal meaning of any spoken language that you hear. You also understand any written language that you see, but you must be touching the surface on which the words are written. It takes about 1 minute to read one page of text.

This spell doesn't decode secret messages in a text or a glyph, such as an arcane sigil, that isn't part of a written language.

materials.value: A pinch of soot and salt

description.value:
Byscilla is a 3rd-level spellcaster. Her spellcasting ability is Charisma (spell save DC 13, +5 to hit with spell attacks). She has the following wizard spells prepared:

Cantrips (at will): fire bolt, light, mage hand, prestidigitation

1st level (4 slots): comprehend languages, detect magic, mage armor, magic missile, shield

2nd level (2 slots): blur, invisibility

Byscilla is a natural born sorceress. Her spellcasting ability is Charisma.

You hurl a mote of fire at a creature or an object within range. Make a ranged spell attack against the target. On a hit, the target takes 1d10 Fire damage. A flammable object hit by this spell starts burning if it isn't being worn or carried.

Cantrip Upgrade. The damage increases by 1d10 when you reach levels 5 (2d10), 11 (3d10), and 17 (4d10).

You create a magical effect within range. Choose the effect from the options below. If you cast this spell multiple times, you can have up to three of its non-instantaneous effects active at a time.

Sensory Effect. You create an instantaneous, harmless sensory effect, such as a shower of sparks, a puff of wind, faint musical notes, or an odd odor.

Fire Play. You instantaneously light or snuff out a candle, a torch, or a small campfire.

Clean or Soil. You instantaneously clean or soil an object no larger than 1 cubic foot.

Minor Sensation. You chill, warm, or flavor up to 1 cubic foot of nonliving material for 1 hour.

Magic Mark. You make a color, a small mark, or a symbol appear on an object or a surface for 1 hour.

Minor Creation. You create a nonmagical trinket or an illusory image that can fit in your hand. It lasts until the end of your next turn. A trinket can deal no damage and has no monetary worth.

For the duration, you sense the presence of magical effects within 30 feet of yourself. If you sense such effects, you can take the Magic action to see a faint aura around any visible creature or object in the area that bears the magic, and if an effect was created by a spell, you learn the spell's school of magic.

The spell is blocked by 1 foot of stone, dirt, or wood; 1 inch of metal; or a thin sheet of lead.

An imperceptible barrier of magical force protects you. Until the start of your next turn, you have a +5 bonus to AC, including against the triggering attack, and you take no damage from @UUID[Compendium.dnd5e.spells24.Item.phbsplMagicMissi]{Magic Missile}.
