The Samurai is a fighter who draws on an implacable fighting spirit to overcome enemies. A Samurai's resolve is nearly unbreakable, and the enemies in a Samurai's path have two choices: yield or die fighting.

Bonus Proficiency

When you choose this archetype at 3rd level, you gain proficiency in one of the following skills of your choice: &Reference[skill=History], &Reference[skill=Insight], &Reference[skill=Performance], or &Reference[skill=Persuasion]. Alternatively, you learn one language of your choice.

Fighting Spirit

Starting at 3rd level, your intensity in battle can shield you and help you strike true. As a bonus action on your turn, you can give yourself advantage on weapon attack rolls until the end of the current turn. When you do so, you also gain 5 temporary hit points. The number of temporary hit points increases when you reach certain levels in this class, increasing to 10 at 10th level and 15 at 15th level.

You can use this feature three times, and you regain all expended uses of it when you finish a long rest.

Elegant Courtier

Starting at 7th level, your discipline and attention to detail allow you to excel in social situations. Whenever you make a Charisma (&Reference[skill=Persuasion]) check, you gain a bonus to the check equal to your Wisdom modifier.

Your self-control also causes you to gain proficiency in Wisdom saving throws. If you already have this proficiency, you instead gain proficiency in Intelligence or Charisma saving throws (your choice).

Tireless Spirit

Starting at 10th level, when you roll initiative and have no uses of Fighting Spirit remaining, you regain one use.

Rapid Strike

Starting at 15th level, you learn to trade accuracy for swift strikes. If you take the @action[Attack] action on your turn and have advantage on an attack roll against one of the targets, you can forgo the advantage for that roll to make an additional weapon attack against that target, as part of the same action. You can do so no more than once per turn.

Strength before Death

Starting at 18th level, your fighting spirit can delay the grasp of death. If you take damage that reduces you to 0 hit points and doesn't kill you outright, you can use your reaction to delay falling &Reference[condition=unconscious], and you can immediately take an extra turn, interrupting the current turn. While you have 0 hit points during that extra turn, taking damage causes death saving throw failures as normal, and three death saving throw failures can still kill you. When the extra turn ends, you fall &Reference[condition=unconscious] if you still have 0 hit points.

Once you use this feature, you can't use it again until you finish a long rest.

Variant: Spell Points

Source: Dungeon Masters Guide

With this variant system, a character who has the Spellcasting feature uses spell points instead spell slots to fuel spells. Spell points give a caster more flexibility, at the cost of greater complexity.

In this variant, each spell has a point cost based on its level. The Spell Point Cost table summarizes the cost in spell points of slots from 1st to 9th level. Cantrips don't require slots and therefore don't require spell points.

Instead of gaining a number of spell slots to cast your spells from the Spellcasting feature, you gain a pool of spell points instead. You expend a number of spell points to create a spell slot of a given level, and then use that slot to cast a spell. You can't reduce your spell points total to less than 0, and you regain all spent spell points when you finish a long rest.

Spells of 6th level and higher are particularly taxing to cast. You can use spell points to create one slot of each level of 6th or higher. You can't create another slot of the same level until you finish a long rest.

The number of spell points you have to spend is based on your level as a spellcaster, as shown in the Spell Points by Level table. Your level also determines the maximum-level spell slot you can create. Even though you might have enough points to create a slot above this maximum, you can't do so.

The Spell Points by Level table applies to bards, clerics, druids, sorcerers, and wizards. For a paladin or ranger, halve the character's level in that class and then consult the table. For a fighter (Eldritch Knight) or rogue (Arcane Trickster), divide the character's level in that class by three. 

For an Artificer, add half your levels (rounded up) in the artificer class to to determine your available spell points. (homebrew)

If woken up from this sleep they instead gain an exhaustion level. If left alone they will sleep until the alcohol runs its course, and awake rested and feeling fresh.

A huge fig-like fruit plucked from the tree growing in the foyer of the Faerie manor. It is fragrant and probably delicious.

Once eaten, you discover that you can read and speak fluent Sylvan for 1 hour.

This long, two-handed weapon is light, the staff portion made of a flexible, woody stem. It is topped with a large flower bud of densely packed petals that are sturdy enough to serve as a bludgeon.

In its default state it deals bludgeoning damage. When this weapon is exposed to daylight (natural or magical) the flower bud blooms, revealing a blade of milky gray steel which is wickedly sharp, and remains open for the rest of the day. The Morning Glory closes itself again when night falls or it spends at least an hour in darkness.

This goblet or cup holds a single serving of red, red wine. It smells sweet as strawberries and potent alcohol.

Any creature drinking this wine must make a DC 15 Constitution saving through or suffer the poisoned condition for an hour. The potent fey magic in the wine ignores immunity.

While the creature remains poisoned they also gain proficiency in performance, as well as half proficiency in any musical instrument they pick up. If they are already proficient they gain expertise instead, and if they have expertise they instead gain advantage on any related checks.

Once the wine wears off the creature gains a level of exhaustion and loses all benefits the wine provided.

Uncommon Consumable. A bottle of extraordinarily expensive wine looted from one of the vampire dinner parties at Raventree Manor during the dimensional chaos of Highsun 16-22, 1040 BF. The label identifies it as a vintage from 687 BF (268 years old), produced in vineyards that no longer exist, from grapes cultivated by vampire lords who appreciated fine wine almost as much as fine blood. The bottle itself is a work of art—hand-blown glass with intricate etchings, sealed with wax bearing the crest of House Raventree.

When you consume this wine (drinking the full bottle takes 1 minute), you gain the following benefits for 1 hour:

  • +2 bonus to Charisma (Persuasion) and Charisma (Deception) checks (the wine's sophistication rubs off on you, somehow)
  • Advantage on saving throws against poison and disease
  • You regain 3d8 + 3 hit points as the enchanted vintage courses through your system
  • You gain darkvision out to 60 feet (if you already have darkvision, its range increases by 30 feet)
  • Your blood becomes mildly toxic to vampires for the duration—any vampire that bites you takes 2d6 necrotic damage as the enchanted wine reacts violently to their digestive process

However, the wine is also strongly associated with vampire magic. For the duration of the effect, you are treated as an undead creature for purposes of spells and effects that specifically target undead (such as Turn Undead, though you're not actually compelled to flee). This is usually not a problem for Wario, who uses the wine purely for its healing and social benefits, but it has caused awkward moments when he's been suddenly affected by a paladin's Turn Undead while trying to negotiate a deal.

Wario has approximately 8 bottles of this wine stolen from Raventree Manor's wine cellars (he would have taken more but they were heavy and he was in a hurry). He treats them as both emergency healing potions and luxury items he can sell to collectors for outrageous prices. He's already sold three bottles for 500-750gp each to merchants who didn't ask questions about provenance, and he's considering raising his prices because "clearly I'm undervaluing rare vintage vampire wine."

The wine actually tastes incredible—rich, complex, with notes of ancient oak, dark fruit, and something faintly metallic that's probably the lingering essence of the vampire blood magic used in its creation. Wario doesn't particularly appreciate fine wine (he drinks it like grape juice), but he recognizes quality when it's profitable.
description.chat: You pop the cork with your teeth—you have absolutely no respect for proper wine-opening etiquette—spit it aside, and take a long swig directly from the bottle. The wine is rich, complex, centuries of careful aging creating flavors you can't quite identify but definitely appreciate on a "this tastes expensive" level. You wipe your mouth with the back of your glove, leaving a purple-red stain. "Good stuff! WAH HA HA!" You take another swig. This is too valuable to waste on savoring, better drink it all now before someone tries to take it.

unidentified.name: Ancient Vintage Wine
unidentified.description: A bottle of extremely old wine with an ornate label in archaic script identifying it as a vintage from 687 BF. The bottle itself is beautiful hand-blown glass with intricate etchings, and the wax seal bears the crest of a noble house. The whole thing is covered in dust and decorative spiderwebs. This is clearly valuable, both as a collector's item and as a consumable of significant magical potency.

description.value: This potion is a magic item. As a Bonus Action, you can drink it or administer it to another creature within 5 feet of yourself. The creature that drinks the magical red fluid in this vial regains 2d4 + 2 Hit Points.

A large bottle of what appears to be high-end brandy found in a fungus-filled closet in the old faerie manor. The brandy within is fragrant and inviting.

This bottle holds about 6 servings of fey brandy in it.

Effect: Upon drinking this brandy a creature must make a successful DC 16 Constitution save against a magical sleep effect. On success the creature gains a level of exhaustion but remains awake, on failure they immediately fall asleep for 1d8 hours.

If woken up from this sleep they instead gain an exhaustion level. If left alone they will sleep until the alcohol runs its course, and awake rested and feeling fresh.

This can effect creatures usually immune to sleep or incapable of sleeping.

A dusty bottle of wine stolen from the cellars of the Feywild Manor during the 'Satyr Eviction' (Day 25). The liquid inside shifts color from green to purple.

Effect: Consuming this wine acts as a Potion of Heroism (10 Temp HP, Bless effect), but for the next hour, the drinker cannot speak without rhyming. Failing to rhyme causes 1d4 psychic damage.
description.chat: Waluigi uncorks the bottle with his teeth. 'Time for a drink, to help me think!'

unidentified.name: Moss-Covered Wine
unidentified.description: A bottle of wine covered in moss. The label is written in Sylvan and moves when you look at it peripherally. It smells like elderberries and mischief.

description.value:
This bright red apple appears entirely harmless, and to the untrained eye there is nothing amiss about it. However, those that have glimpsed it's magical nature know that it harbors a dangerous poison.

Eating this entire apple would deal (42) 12d6 poison damage to the creature that did, and provides no nutrition whatsoever.

This apple can be divided up, which causes the damage to be divided among the pieces. A single slice of apple deals 1d6 poison damage, while half an apple would deal 6d6 poison damage, and so forth.
A slim iron key they probably unlocked a cabinet, chest, or something similar.

A trio of orange crystals that gleam with faerie energy and looks like a perpetual sunset. Touching them makes the fingertips tingle when, and imparts a lightheaded sensation not unlike being inebriated while they are held.

Rare Item (Authenticity Questionable). A stained piece of parchment covered in recipe instructions, measurements, and what appear to be flour handprints. Wario claims this is the original, authentic recipe for Princess Peach's legendary cake—the cake that was so delicious it became famous throughout the Mushroom Kingdom before the war, served at royal functions, and considered one of the great culinary achievements of the pre-war era.

The recipe is written in elegant script (too elegant to be Wario's handwriting), with detailed instructions for a multi-layered strawberry cake with cream filling and decorative frosting. The measurements are in pre-war Mushroom Kingdom units, and there are marginal notes like "His Majesty preferred extra strawberries" and "Princess requests heart-shaped decoration for festivals."

The parchment shows significant age—yellowed edges, small tears, stains from what might be actual cake ingredients (or might just be random kitchen spills from whoever actually wrote this). There's a royal seal watermark visible when held up to light, which Wario points to as "proof of authenticity."

If the recipe is actually followed: Make an Intelligence check (using Cook's Utensils proficiency if you have it). On a 15 or higher, you successfully create a cake that is genuinely delicious—anyone who eats a slice regains 2d4+2 hit points and gains advantage on Charisma checks for 1 hour as they're put in a wonderful mood by the exceptional taste. On a 10-14, you create a good but not spectacular cake that provides the healing but not the Charisma bonus. On a 9 or lower, something goes wrong and you waste the ingredients.

The Authenticity Question: Wario acquired this recipe during a looting expedition to the ruins of Peach's castle sometime around 1005 BF. He claims he found it in the royal kitchens, sealed in a waterproof container, preserved perfectly for exactly this purpose. Skeptics point out that:

  • The parchment's age is inconsistent—it looks old, but not 85+ years old
  • The royal seal watermark matches Peach-era documentation, but Wario could have stolen blank royal stationery and written this himself
  • Several ingredients listed didn't become available in the Mushroom Kingdom until after Peach's death, suggesting the recipe was written later
  • Wario has been caught selling "authentic royal recipes" before, most notably "Bowser's Secret Fire Flower Chili Recipe" which turned out to be copied from a common cookbook with "add more heat" scribbled in the margins

Wario refuses to address these inconsistencies, insisting the recipe is genuine and pricing it at 5,000 gold pieces for interested buyers ("It's a piece of history! Priceless! I'm practically giving it away at 5,000!"). He's also created multiple "certified copies" that he sells for 500 gold pieces each, claiming they're "authorized reproductions" (they're just transcriptions he made himself).

The truth is ambiguous: the recipe might be authentic, might be a skilled forgery, or might be a real recipe that Wario found and is now wildly exaggerating the provenance of. The cake it produces is genuinely good regardless of authenticity, which Wario considers the only fact that matters ("Does it matter WHERE the recipe came from if the cake tastes amazing? No! Stop asking questions and pay me!").
description.chat: You carefully unfold the parchment, treating it with exaggerated reverence as if it's a sacred relic. "Behold! The ORIGINAL recipe for Princess Peach's legendary cake! Used at royal banquets! Tasted by kings! Queens! That plumber guy!" You point at the flour handprints with pride. "See? These are probably Peach's ACTUAL handprints! Priceless! Historical artifact! You can't put a price on history! But if you could, it would be 5,000 gold pieces! Final offer! Non-negotiable!" You're already mentally spending the money before they've even agreed to buy it.

unidentified.description: A yellowed piece of parchment containing a detailed cake recipe with elegant handwriting, marginal notes, and what appear to be flour handprints. There's a watermark visible when held to light that might be a royal seal. The recipe looks old and valuable, though verifying its claimed provenance would require expert analysis. Someone is clearly trying to sell this as more than just a cake recipe.

This wooden weapon is sprouted from a roughly fistsized seed that's still attached to its base. A large, red thorn creates the weapon's pointed tip. Dense, thorny vines coil around the top and bottom of the haft, with small, glowing splits appearing in the wood beneath them. You gain a +1 bonus to attack and damage rolls made with this magic weapon.

In addition, this weapon has 5 charges and regains all expended charges daily at dawn. When you make a ranged attack with the weapon, you can choose to expend 1 of its charges. Hit or miss, the weapon explodes into thorny shrapnel after it reaches the target. The target and each creature within 10 feet of it must make a DC 15 Dexterity saving throw. A creatures takes [[/damage 1d8 type=piercing]] damage on a failed save, or half as much damage on a successful one. If the target was hit by the attack, it automatically fails the saving throw. Immediately after the weapon explodes, the seed reappears at your location and regrows the weapon into your hand.

The housebound can move through a space as narrow as 1 inch wide without squeezing. It is also immune to being restrained or grappled.

The housebound can move through objects as if they were difficult terrain.

The housebound can perfectly meld with any medium sized inanimate object, or within walls. The only requirement is that the wall space be in dim light or darkness when they enter.

While merged with this object they cannot be detected with normal senses. The Housebound can remain on that surface as long as they want, and can move along it to any connected surfaces or objects large enough to hold them.

The housebound can hide invisibly on the surface of most objects.
While in sunlight, the housebound has disadvantage on attack rolls, ability checks, and saving throws.

Melee Weapon Attack: +5 to hit, 5 ft., one creature. Hit: 10 (2d6 + 3) slashing damage.

The housebound attacks with its shadowy claws, rending flesh with horrible ease.
In the first round of a combat, the Housebound has advantage on attack rolls against any creature it has surprised.

The Housebound is visible if its reflection can be seen in a mirror or other reflective surface. The Housebound appears as a monochromatically skinned bipedal humanoid with an interlaced web of scars covering its flesh.

biography.value:
Koopa Troopa — The Backbone Nobody Thanks

The Koopa Troopa is the standard infantry soldier of the Koopa Troop, the bipedal turtle-people who have served as Bowser's primary ground forces for as long as anyone can remember. They walk patrol routes. They man fortress positions. They stand between Mario and whatever objective Mario is stomping toward. And they die—in enormous numbers, with depressing regularity, respawning through mechanisms that nobody fully understands and that the koopas themselves describe only as "it's a turtle thing."

The average Koopa Troopa is not stupid, despite what the legends suggest. The average Koopa Troopa is a conscript or career soldier who signed on with the Troop because Darkland's economy offers limited alternatives and because Bowser's military provides food, shelter, and a shell-maintenance stipend that civilian life cannot match. They follow orders because the chain of command works, because the alternative is court martial, and because most of them genuinely believe in the Koopa Troop's mission even if they can't quite articulate what that mission is now that Bowser has been absent for weeks and Kamek is issuing orders that don't match what Bowser would have wanted.

Kamek's return to the Valley of Bowser on Highsun 18 has created a command crisis that the rank-and-file Koopa Troopas are navigating with the specific anxiety of soldiers who know something is wrong but don't have enough information to know what. Kamek is giving orders. The orders are legal under Troop command structure. But the orders don't feel right—they're focused on consolidation and control rather than rescue, on securing Kamek's position rather than finding Bowser, on preparing for something that Kamek hasn't explained. The Troopas follow because following is what they do. Some of them are starting to wonder whether what they do and what they should do have diverged.
biography.public: A bipedal turtle in standard Koopa Troop equipment, walking a patrol route with the resigned competence of someone who has been doing this job long enough to know it's thankless but not long enough to quit.

description.value:
Every koopa is born with a shell, and every koopa's shell tells the story of their life. Standard Troopa shells are green, smooth, and maintained according to Troop regulations that specify acceptable polish levels, damage repair protocols, and the specific angle at which rank insignia should be painted. A well-maintained shell is a source of pride. A damaged shell is a source of shame. A lost shell is a tragedy that most koopas would rather not discuss.

The shell provides AC 15 (natural armor) and allows the signature koopa defensive maneuver: withdrawal. As an action, a Koopa Troopa can withdraw fully into its shell, becoming a small, hard object with AC 18 and resistance to all damage except psychic. While withdrawn, the koopa cannot take actions, bonus actions, or reactions, and its speed is 0. Emerging from the shell requires a bonus action on a subsequent turn.

A withdrawn koopa can also be kicked, thrown, or otherwise used as a projectile by creatures strong enough to lift it. This is considered extremely rude in koopa culture and extremely effective in combat, dealing 2d6 bludgeoning damage to whatever the shell hits and 1d6 bludgeoning damage to the koopa inside.
description.chat: The shell is home, armor, and identity all in one. Taking care of it is the first thing a Troopa learns. Getting kicked while inside it is a risk they accepted when they signed up.

unidentified.name: Green Koopa Shell
unidentified.description: A natural shell that provides significant protection and allows full withdrawal for enhanced defense. The shell shows signs of regulation maintenance.

description.value: A standard-issue spear provided to Koopa Troop infantry, designed for koopa proportions and fighting styles. The spear is slightly shorter than human equivalent weapons, compensating for koopas' smaller stature while maintaining adequate reach to threaten enemies before they get close enough to stomp. The spearhead is mass-produced in Darkland foundries with quality that is adequate without being impressive—sharp enough for combat, durable enough for field conditions, replaceable enough that losing one doesn't require paperwork that takes longer than the battle did.
description.chat: Standard issue, standard quality, standard pointing-end-toward-enemy training. The spear does its job because the Troopa behind it does theirs.

unidentified.name: Military Spear
unidentified.description: A standard-issue spear of adequate quality, designed for small humanoid proportions.

description.value:
A Koopa Troopa can withdraw into its shell and launch itself at an enemy as a spinning projectile, sliding across the ground in a straight line up to 20 feet. One creature in the path must make a DC 12 Dexterity saving throw, taking 2d6 bludgeoning damage on a failure or half on a success. After the spin, the Troopa emerges from its shell in the space at the end of the movement, prone, and cannot take reactions until the start of its next turn.

The shell spin is the Troop's signature combat technique—every recruit learns it during basic training, practices it until the timing is automatic, and uses it in combat with the specific commitment of someone who knows that turning yourself into a projectile has inherent risks but also knows that the alternative is being stomped by something larger than you.
description.chat: The shell spins across the ground with the commitment of someone who has accepted that being a living cannonball is part of the job description.

description.value:
Koopa Troopas currently serve under Kamek's consolidated command following Bowser's extended absence. They follow orders because the chain of command requires it, but growing unease about Kamek's priorities—consolidation over rescue, control over search—has created a morale situation that could be exploited by parties who understand koopa loyalty structures.

Koopa Troopas who learn that Bowser is alive and that someone is actively trying to reach him become significantly more sympathetic to that someone's cause. A DC 13 Charisma (Persuasion) check can convince a Troopa to share information about Kamek's operations, patrol schedules, or defensive positions if the party demonstrates genuine intent to help Bowser. A DC 16 check can convince a Troopa to actively assist, though the assistance will be limited by the Troopa's fear of Kamek's magical capabilities.

Koopas who served directly under Bowser—veterans who remember his personal leadership rather than Kamek's proxy authority—are easier to turn (DC reduces by 3) because their loyalty is to the king rather than the institution.
description.chat: They follow Kamek because the rules say follow Kamek. They'd follow Bowser because their hearts say follow Bowser. The gap between rules and hearts is where opportunities live.

biography.value:
Era sheet: Highsun 1, 955 BF, Peach's Castle. Art and stats describe this figure on the night of the Day Of (events.json highsun_1_955_bf_the_day_of), not the present day of the campaign (1040 BF).

Scene kit — The Interloper at the Council. Bowser and his force burst in on a crucial palace meeting. This is a GM scene kit, not a filed event; nothing on this sheet changes the canon record of what happened that night.

Elite Koopa in full dark-steel plate, spiked helm, spiked pauldrons, spiked shell, black halberd. The ones who walk in behind Bowser and stand at the doors so nobody leaves the meeting early.

description.value: Reach. Heavy, two-handed.
The Koopatrol makes two Halberd attacks.
A creature that grapples the Koopatrol or hits it with an unarmed strike takes 1d6 piercing damage.
The Koopatrol moves through the spaces of allied Troop units freely, and allies directly behind it have half cover against ranged attacks.
Kryn is an 18th-level spellcaster. His spellcasting ability is Charisma (spell save DC 17, +9 to hit with spell attacks).

You hurl a mote of fire at a creature or an object within range. Make a ranged spell attack against the target. On a hit, the target takes 1d10 Fire damage. A flammable object hit by this spell starts burning if it isn't being worn or carried.

Cantrip Upgrade. The damage increases by 1d10 when you reach levels 5 (2d10), 11 (3d10), and 17 (4d10).

A spectral, floating hand appears at a point you choose within range. The hand lasts for the duration. The hand vanishes if it is ever more than 30 feet away from you or if you cast this spell again.

When you cast the spell, you can use the hand to manipulate an object, open an unlocked door or container, stow or retrieve an item from an open container, or pour the contents out of a vial.

As a Magic action on your later turns, you can control the hand thus again. As part of that action, you can move the hand up to 30 feet.

The hand can't attack, activate magic items, or carry more than 10 pounds.

You create a magical effect within range. Choose the effect from the options below. If you cast this spell multiple times, you can have up to three of its non-instantaneous effects active at a time.

Sensory Effect. You create an instantaneous, harmless sensory effect, such as a shower of sparks, a puff of wind, faint musical notes, or an odd odor.

Fire Play. You instantaneously light or snuff out a candle, a torch, or a small campfire.

Clean or Soil. You instantaneously clean or soil an object no larger than 1 cubic foot.

Minor Sensation. You chill, warm, or flavor up to 1 cubic foot of nonliving material for 1 hour.

Magic Mark. You make a color, a small mark, or a symbol appear on an object or a surface for 1 hour.

Minor Creation. You create a nonmagical trinket or an illusory image that can fit in your hand. It lasts until the end of your next turn. A trinket can deal no damage and has no monetary worth.

For the duration, you sense the presence of magical effects within 30 feet of yourself. If you sense such effects, you can take the Magic action to see a faint aura around any visible creature or object in the area that bears the magic, and if an effect was created by a spell, you learn the spell's school of magic.

The spell is blocked by 1 foot of stone, dirt, or wood; 1 inch of metal; or a thin sheet of lead.

You attempt to interrupt a creature in the process of casting a spell. The creature makes a Constitution saving throw. On a failed save, the spell dissipates with no effect, and the action, Bonus Action, or Reaction used to cast it is wasted. If that spell was cast with a spell slot, the slot isn't expended.

In addition, whenever a creature within 5 feet of you hits you with a melee attack roll, the shield erupts with flame. The attacker takes [[/damage 2d8 type=fire]] damage from a warm shield or [[/damage 2d8 type=cold]] damage from a chill shield.

On a failed save, the spell creates an Invisible, intangible sensor within 10 feet of the target. You can see and hear through the sensor as if you were there. The sensor moves with the target, remaining within 10 feet of it for the duration. If something can see the sensor, it appears as a luminous orb about the size of your fist.

An Invisible wall of force springs into existence at a point you choose within range. The wall appears in any orientation you choose, as a horizontal or vertical barrier or at an angle. It can be free floating or resting on a solid surface. You can form it into a hemispherical dome or a globe with a radius of up to 10 feet, or you can shape a flat surface made up of ten 10-foot-by-10-foot panels. Each panel must be contiguous with another panel. In any form, the wall is 1/4 inch thick and lasts for the duration. If the wall cuts through a creature's space when it appears, the creature is pushed to one side of the wall (you choose which side).

Nothing can physically pass through the wall. It is immune to all damage and can't be dispelled by @UUID[Compendium.dnd5e.spells24.Item.phbsplDispelMagi]{Dispel Magic}. A @UUID[Compendium.dnd5e.spells24.Item.phbsplDisintegra]{Disintegrate} spell destroys the wall instantly, however. The wall also extends into the Ethereal Plane and blocks ethereal travel through the wall.
Briefly surrounded by silvery mist, you teleport up to 30 feet to an unoccupied space you can see.

You teleport yourself from your current location to any other spot within range. You arrive at exactly the spot desired. It can be a place you can see, one you can visualize, or one you can describe by stating distance and direction, such as "200 feet straight downward" or "upward to the northwest at a 45-degree angle, 300 feet."

You can bring along objects as long as their weight doesn't exceed what you can carry. You can also bring one willing creature of your size or smaller who is carrying gear up to its carrying capacity. The creature must be within 5 feet of you when you cast this spell.

If you would arrive in a place already occupied by an object or a creature, you and any creature traveling with you each take 4d6 force damage, and the spell fails to teleport you.

Kryn manipulates his spell, quickening its casting method!

When Kryn casts a spell that forces a creature to make a saving throw to resist its effects, you can spend 3 sorcery points to give one target of the spell disadvantage on its first saving throw made against the spell.

Kryn heightens the magic of his spell, causing its effects to be more difficult to resist.

When Kryn casts a spell that deals fire or lightning damage, he can change the damage type to one of the following damage types instead: acid, fire, lightning. Aside from the type of damage done, the spell functions otherwise as normal.

This costs 2 spell points and cannot be combined with the effects of Twin or Quicken spell. After use, the power recharges on a 3.

Kryn warps the magical energy forming around him, changing some elemental nature about it!

You hurl three fiery rays. You can hurl them at one target within range or at several. Make a ranged spell attack for each ray. On a hit, the target takes 2d6 Fire damage.

Covering the object with something opaque blocks the light. The spell ends if you cast it again.

You speak a one-word command to a creature you can see within range. The target must succeed on a Wisdom saving throw or follow the command on its next turn. Choose the command from these options:

Approach. The target moves toward you by the shortest and most direct route, ending its turn if it moves within 5 feet of you.

Drop. The target drops whatever it is holding and then ends its turn.

Three illusory duplicates of yourself appear in your space. Until the spell ends, the duplicates move with you and mimic your actions, shifting position so it's impossible to track which image is real.

Each time a creature hits you with an attack roll during the spell's duration, roll a [[/r (@flags.dnd-players-handbook.mirrorImages)d6kh1cs>2#Duplicate destroyed]]{d6 for each} of your remaining duplicates. If any of the d6s rolls a 3 or higher, one of the duplicates is hit instead of you, and the duplicate is destroyed. The duplicates otherwise ignore all other damage and effects. A creature is unaffected by this spell if it has the &Reference[blinded apply=false] condition, &Reference[blindsight], or &Reference[truesight].

The target has Advantage on the save if you or your allies are fighting it. Whenever the target takes damage, it repeats the save, ending the spell on itself on a success.

You have a telepathic link with the Charmed target while the two of you are on the same plane of existence. On your turn, you can use this link to issue commands to the target (no action required), such as "Attack that creature," "Move over there," or "Fetch that object."
