A broken half‑ring of blackened gold with a dull, cracked red gem that still pulses faintly with command‑magic. This was once the "handler" half of a paired Entropy Ring system like the one the Iron Legion forced onto Toadburt on Highsun 21, turning him into a coerced sleeper agent with a three‑day deadline to capture the Oracle. Archie managed to snap this handler piece off during his own interrogation by Agent Malissia in the physical antechamber, intending to study it and reverse‑engineer a way to free those bound by the complete rings.

He never got the chance. But even broken, the ring stub retains enough residual magic to sense its paired counterparts and—just once per day—to jam their signal. This is how Archie hoped to give Toadburt one moment of free will, one chance to disobey the Iron Legion's orders and act as himself instead of their puppet. Whether Toadburt ever received that chance, or whether the jamming came too late, is a question the stub cannot answer. It can only pulse with the distant heartbeat of command‑magic still being transmitted somewhere in the world.

While attuned, you can sense if an active Entropy Ring is within 300 feet. You learn only "near" or "farther than that," but not direction or who wears it. Once per day, as an action, you can focus on the stub and attempt to jam an Entropy Ring in range. The bearer of that ring must succeed on a DC 14 Wisdom saving throw or experience 1 round of static in their orders—they know something is wrong and briefly act under their own will instead of their controller's. Each time you use the jamming effect, you must succeed on a DC 12 Constitution save or take 1d6 necrotic damage as the broken magic eats at your fingertips, aging them visibly for a few heartbeats.
description.chat: The cracked gem buzzes with distant command‑magic, like half of a conversation you can barely hear.

unidentified.name: Cracked Red Gem Ring
unidentified.description: A broken half‑circle ring ending in a cracked red stone. It feels heavier than it looks, and the gold has been blackened as though exposed to intense magical discharge. The gem occasionally pulses with a dim internal light, always in irregular rhythms that suggest some kind of coded signal being transmitted to or from an unknown source.

description.value:
A rolled‑up parchment, singed at the edges and smelling faintly of sulfur, depicting the destroyed Raventree greenhouse in meticulous top‑down view. Tiny colored ink circles mark where each rust monster died, with precise measurements of blast radii, casualty vectors, and structural collapse patterns. The corner is labeled in Archie's increasingly frantic hand: 'Proof this was Tactically Justified.' This is the "evidence" Archie compiled immediately after the Greenhouse Inferno on Highsun 17, attempting to retroactively prove that his overcharged Fireball was the only way to save the party from the rust monster swarm.

He referenced this document when he went on Wahbook on Highsun 20 to publicly confess and justify his actions, arguing with cold mathematical precision that he had saved more lives than he'd taken. The diagram is half combat analysis—noting optimal engagement angles and acceptable casualty thresholds—and half self‑absolution, with margin notes like "No other option" and "They would have done the same." The Mages' Guild saw it as damning evidence of reckless endangerment. The Liberated Toads saw themselves marked as "acceptable collateral." Archie saw it as proof he was right, even if being right cost him everything.

A spellcaster who spends a short rest studying the diagram can apply its cold tactical lessons once: the next time they cast an area fire spell, they can choose any number of creatures up to their spellcasting modifier to automatically succeed on the save against that spell, though they still take half damage. Any Liberated Toad who sees their own location marked as "acceptable collateral" must succeed on a DC 12 Wisdom save or be consumed by anger toward Archie's memory for the rest of the day, unable to speak positively of him or his actions.
description.chat: Colored blast‑circles, casualty marks, and tiny scribbles — the greenhouse as seen through Archie's cold, tactical eye.

unidentified.name: Scorched Floorplan
unidentified.description: A partially burned blueprint of a glass‑roofed building, annotated with circles and numbers in multiple colors of ink. The draftsmanship is precise despite the damage, and small notations in cramped handwriting fill every available margin. Scorch marks along the edges suggest this document was itself present during whatever fire it depicts, and you can still smell smoke when you unroll it.

description.value:
A tarnished brass circlet lined with a strip of stiff, dried leather that bears the faint chemical smell of alchemical preservation. On the inside, written in Archie's cramped ink, is a desperate mantra: 'The eye sees across – the band keeps me from falling in.' Faint grooves mark where the metal dug into his brow during the unstable Third Eye Escape on Highsun 20, when he traversed alien dimensions to evade capture. The band itself vibrates faintly when brought near mirrors or planar boundaries, as though resonating with tears in reality.

This circlet represents Archie's personal safeguard against the very magic he studied. After encountering his own two‑eyed clone in the sewers beneath the restaurant on Highsun 14—a clone desperate to steal his third eye for the Iron Legion's necromancers—Archie became obsessed with protecting his mind from dimensional fracture. The band is his answer: crude, painful, but effective. It kept him anchored during his escape through the Deep Layers and prevented the Oracle's fractured visions from consuming him entirely during the Shattered Ritual.

While attuned and worn, you gain a +1 bonus to Intelligence (Arcana) checks and Wisdom (Perception) checks involving portals, planar anomalies, mirrors, or time distortions. Once per long rest, when you would suffer a teleportation mishap, become Banished, or be pulled into an extra‑dimensional space against your will, you can use your reaction to negate that effect for yourself. Each time you use this reaction, you gain one level of Short‑Term Madness as you momentarily see the fractured timelines the way Archie did—Physical, Shadow, Fey, and Deep Mirror all overlapping in impossible geometries.
description.chat: The band squeezes around your temples, and for a second the room triple‑exposes into Physical, Mirror, and Deep Layers before snapping back.

unidentified.name: Tight Brass Circlet
unidentified.description: A plain brass band, slightly warped, with ink‑scribbles along the inner rim. It feels uncomfortable, like it's meant to be too tight. The leather lining is stiff and cracked, and there are faint pressure marks on the inside as though someone wore this for extended periods despite the discomfort. When you hold it up to the light, the brass seems to shimmer with an oil‑slick iridescence.

The Rotting Skull Piercer is a nightmarish warhammer forged from the calcified skull of an ancient lich, its surface etched with arcane runes that pulse with a sickly green ichor. When wielded, it unleashes waves of decaying energy that corrode both flesh and metal, leaving nothing but bone behind. Its touch is said to spread rot through the very air, making those who hold it feel as though their own vitality is being consumed.

Effects

  • Rotting Decay: On activation, the Rotting Skull Piercer unleashes a wave of decaying energy that deals 100 points of damage over five turns. The target must make a DC 18 Constitution saving throw or be affected by the 'Rotting' status effect, which reduces their armor class by 2 until the end of their next turn.
  • Armor Corrosion: Each time you hit with this weapon, there is a 30% chance that the target is also inflicted with 'Weakness,' reducing its Strength score by 1 for one minute. This effect stacks up to three times per encounter.

Usage

  • Activation: Action
  • Duration: Instantaneous effect over five turns
  • Ends when: The target successfully saves against Rotting Decay or the weapon is used again on a different target.
  • Charges: Unlimited, recharged at dawn

The Skullsplitter Warhammer, forged from the bones of fallen soldiers, exudes a dark, almost sentient power. Its haft is reinforced with iron bands and its head is adorned with an ancient rune that whispers malevolent secrets to those who wield it. This weapon guarantees a crushing blow, capable of turning the strongest foe into dust with each strike. However, those who use it must beware, for it seems to have a mind of its own, often striking out at unintended targets in its fervor to destroy.

Effects

If the target is reduced to half its hit points or fewer by this weapon, there is a 50% chance that they bleed out and take an additional 1d4 necrotic damage at the start of their next turn.
  • Sentient Wrath: At the end of each of your turns while wielding the Skullsplitter Warhammer, there is a 25% chance that it will lash out and target an enemy within 5 feet of you. This attack deals 1d8 bludgeoning damage and has disadvantage if you are concentrating or using an action.

Usage

  • Activation: As a bonus action
  • Duration: Until the start of your next turn
  • Ends when: You sheathe it or drop the weapon, or if you take an action other than moving
  • Charges: Unlimited

Midbus — Fawful's Fist, Bowser's Replacement

Midbus is the creature Fawful built to be Bowser's opposite. Where Bowser is fire, Midbus is ice. Where Bowser is prideful rage, Midbus is cold obedience. Where Bowser fights for his own glory, Midbus fights because Fawful tells him to fight. He is a massive pig-beast of uncertain origin—part mechanical, part organic, part something that Fawful's engineering produced through processes that conventional biology finds objectionable—and he serves as Fawful's primary enforcer, bodyguard, and blunt instrument for situations that require something larger than bombs and more reliable than dragons.

The relationship between Midbus and Fawful is the inverse of the relationship between Bowser and his Koopa Troop. The Koopa Troop follows Bowser because he's powerful and because loyalty to the king is tradition. Midbus follows Fawful because Fawful MADE him. Not in the biological sense—Midbus existed before Fawful found him—but in every functional sense. Fawful took something large, stupid, and violent and gave it purpose, direction, and the modifications necessary to become something genuinely dangerous rather than merely big. Without Fawful, Midbus would be an animal. With Fawful, Midbus is a weapon that happens to have a personality, though the personality consists primarily of loyalty and the desire to hit things hard enough that they stop moving.

Midbus's modifications are extensive and not entirely visible. The ice capabilities that define his combat style are not natural—they were installed by Fawful using technology derived from the Dark Star fragment and Beanish cryogenic engineering that was considered too dangerous for military application by the Beanbean Kingdom's regulators. Fawful didn't care about regulators. Fawful cared about results. The result is a creature that can generate freezing temperatures from its body, project ice in offensive formations, and sustain itself in environments that would kill organic beings through cold alone.

The "Blizzard Fist" designation is Fawful's invention—he names everything, he names it dramatically, and he expects the names to be used. Midbus doesn't care about the name. Midbus doesn't care about most things. He cares about following Fawful's orders, eating large quantities of food, and proving that he is stronger than Bowser. The last motivation is the only one that produces genuine emotional response—when Bowser's name is mentioned, Midbus's normally placid demeanor shifts to something approaching engagement, and his already considerable aggression intensifies to levels that make Fawful's other operatives nervous.

The rivalry with Bowser predates Fawful's current operation. During the Dark Star Crisis—an event that official records minimize even more aggressively than they minimize the Chaos Heart Crisis—Midbus and Bowser fought repeatedly, each encounter escalating in destruction and personal animosity. Midbus won some of these fights. Bowser won others. Neither achieved the decisive victory that would end the rivalry, and both carry the frustration of unfinished business that only another fight can resolve.

Currently, Midbus serves as the garrison commander of Peach's Castle under Fawful's occupation. He manages the five hundred-plus troops, maintains order among personnel whose loyalty to Fawful varies from genuine devotion to practical opportunism, and deals with the logistical challenges of occupying a castle that was designed for royal residence rather than military fortification. His management style is straightforward: follow orders or be hurt. The simplicity works because Midbus can back it up, and because soldiers who've seen what happens to people who disobey Midbus tend to become enthusiastic followers very quickly.

The four Operation HOMECOMING operatives embedded in Fawful's servant staff operate under Midbus's garrison command without his knowledge. If he discovered them, the response would not involve interrogation or political calculation. It would involve Midbus picking them up and throwing them into walls until the walls or the operatives stopped being solid. Midbus doesn't do subtlety. Midbus does kinetic problem-solving, and he considers most problems solvable if you apply enough kinetic energy to them.

If the party encounters Midbus—through the HOMECOMING operation, through direct assault on Peach's Castle, or through the chaotic convergences that have characterized the current crisis—they will face something that combines the raw physical power of a creature designed to match Bowser with the cold-based enhancement of Fawful's forbidden engineering. He is not clever. He is not subtle. He is not interested in conversation beyond confirming that you are an enemy and therefore something to be frozen and broken.

He is, however, loyal. Absolutely, unquestioningly, terminally loyal to Fawful. This loyalty is Midbus's defining characteristic and his most dangerous quality, because it means he will never stop, never negotiate, never question orders, and never accept defeat while Fawful's will requires him to fight. He is the blunt instrument that Fawful's sharp mind deploys when precision has finished its work and what remains requires force.
biography.public: A massive pig-beast wreathed in frost, standing with the planted solidity of something that has been designed to absorb punishment and return it multiplied. His eyes carry the dull patience of someone who is waiting for permission to destroy something.

description.value:
Midbus's primary weapons are his fists—enormous, frost-coated, and capable of delivering impacts that combine raw physical force with cryogenic damage that freezes tissue on contact. The frost isn't external coating; it radiates from within Midbus's modified physiology, generated by the Beanish cryogenic systems that Fawful installed during the modification process. The frost forms continuously, creating a visible layer of ice crystals on Midbus's knuckles that shatters on impact and reforms between punches.

Each strike delivers bludgeoning damage from the physical impact plus cold damage from the cryogenic effect. Targets hit must contend with the freezing effect—the cold numbs flesh, slows reactions, and can immobilize limbs if sustained exposure accumulates. Watching Midbus fight is like watching an avalanche with opinions: large, cold, absolutely committed to reaching the bottom regardless of what's in the way.
description.chat: Frost-coated fists the size of dinner plates swing with force that promises broken bones and frostbite delivered simultaneously.

unidentified.name: Frost-Generating Fists
unidentified.description: Enormous fists that radiate cold from within, delivering both physical and cryogenic damage on impact.

description.value:
Midbus can hurl his considerable mass at enemies, launching himself across distances that something his size shouldn't be able to cover and landing with impact that shakes the ground. The body slam is his answer to enemies who attempt to maintain distance—ranged attackers, spellcasters, anyone who thinks being far away from the pig-beast makes them safe. It doesn't. Nothing makes you safe from something that weighs half a ton and is willing to use itself as a projectile.

As an action, Midbus can move up to 30 feet in a straight line and slam into a creature at the end of the movement. The target must make a DC 19 Strength saving throw. On a failure, the target takes 4d10 + 7 bludgeoning damage plus 2d8 cold damage, is knocked prone, and is pushed 15 feet away from Midbus. On a success, the target takes half damage and is not knocked prone or pushed. The ground in a 10-foot radius around the impact point becomes difficult terrain covered in frost until the end of Midbus's next turn.
description.chat: Half a ton of frozen pig-beast leaves the ground, crosses distance that should be safe, and lands on you. The ground cracks. You crack. The frost seals the cracks shut.

unidentified.name: Devastating Charge
unidentified.description: This creature can launch itself at enemies over significant distance, delivering devastating impact enhanced with cold damage.

description.value: Midbus makes three Blizzard Fist attacks, or one Body Slam and one Blizzard Fist attack. He can replace one Blizzard Fist attack with a Frost Breath if it's available.
description.chat: Three impacts in rapid succession, each one cold enough to freeze and heavy enough to shatter what it freezes.

description.value:
Midbus exhales a blast of supercooled air in a 40-foot cone, freezing everything in its path. The breath isn't natural—it's generated by the cryogenic systems Fawful installed, channeled through Midbus's respiratory system and expelled with the force of his massive lungs. The temperature drops so dramatically that moisture in the air crystallizes instantly, creating a visible cloud of ice particles that obscures vision and coats everything in frost.

Each creature in the cone must make a DC 19 Constitution saving throw. On a failure, a creature takes 10d8 cold damage and has its speed reduced to 0 until the end of its next turn as frost encases its legs and lower body. On a success, a creature takes half damage and its speed is reduced by half instead of being eliminated. Objects in the cone that aren't being worn or carried freeze solid—water becomes ice, metal becomes brittle, organic material crystallizes and can be shattered by subsequent impacts.

The breath weapon's recharge is mechanical rather than biological—the cryogenic systems need time to build sufficient cold before another discharge. The charging process produces visible condensation around Midbus's mouth and a low humming from the systems in his modified chest cavity, warning observant enemies that the breath is about to happen again.
description.chat: Cold erupts from his mouth in a wave that turns air to crystal, water to stone, and courage to the sudden realization that you should have stood somewhere else.

description.value:
Midbus's body continuously generates a layer of ice that forms over his skin, creating natural armor that regenerates as fast as it's broken. The ice is approximately two inches thick at its heaviest points—shoulders, chest, skull—and provides substantial protection against physical attacks. Weapons that strike Midbus often lodge in the ice rather than penetrating to flesh, requiring the attacker to wrench them free while Midbus is already swinging his next attack.

The cryogenic armor provides AC 18 (natural armor) and grants immunity to cold damage as the ice layer absorbs and disperses freezing effects harmlessly. However, the armor creates vulnerability to fire damage—heat melts the ice faster than it can reform, temporarily reducing Midbus's protection and causing the cryogenic systems to overwork in an attempt to compensate. Fire damage against Midbus is doubled, and for 1 round after taking fire damage, his AC decreases by 2 as the armor thins.

The ice also makes Midbus's surroundings cold. Creatures within 5 feet of Midbus at the start of their turn take 1d6 cold damage from proximity to his frozen exterior, and the ground within 10 feet of his position becomes lightly frosted, requiring careful footing from creatures not accustomed to icy surfaces.
description.chat: Ice forms over his body like a second skin, cracking and reforming with each impact, turning him into something that's more glacier than pig.

description.value:
Midbus's only genuine emotional investment beyond loyalty to Fawful is his rivalry with Bowser. The rivalry is visceral, personal, and rooted in the fundamental question of which creature is the supreme physical force in the Mushroom Kingdom's sphere of influence. Midbus was designed to be Bowser's equal and opposite: ice to fire, obedience to pride, cold efficiency to burning rage. Every fight between them has been inconclusive, and the lack of resolution gnaws at Midbus in ways that nothing else reaches.

When Midbus encounters Bowser or learns of Bowser's presence nearby, his behavior changes. The dull patience that normally characterizes his demeanor sharpens into focused aggression. His attacks become more powerful but less disciplined—advantage on damage rolls, disadvantage on attack rolls—as the desire to prove superiority overrides the mechanical precision that Fawful's modifications normally provide. He will prioritize engaging Bowser over any other objective, including Fawful's orders, which represents the only circumstance under which Midbus's loyalty to Fawful takes second place to personal motivation.

Fawful knows about this vulnerability and has historically exploited it—using Bowser's presence as bait to position Midbus where Fawful needs him, channeling the rivalry's energy toward strategic objectives. Whether Fawful considers the rivalry a useful tool or a concerning limitation in his most valuable enforcer is unclear. Knowing Fawful, the answer is probably both.
description.chat: Bowser's name lands in his ears and something behind the dull eyes ignites—the only fire this frozen creature carries, burning with the need to prove who is strongest.

description.value:
Once per day, Midbus can overclock his cryogenic systems, transforming into a larger, more heavily armored version of himself encased in thick ice that extends his reach and amplifies his cold-generating capabilities. The transformation takes 1 round, during which Midbus cannot take actions or reactions as the ice builds around him in layers. The resulting Blizzard Form lasts for 1 minute.

In Blizzard Form, Midbus's size increases from Large to Huge. His reach increases from 5 feet to 10 feet. His Blizzard Fist damage increases to 3d10 + 7 bludgeoning plus 3d8 cold. His Cryogenic Armor's AC increases to 20. The proximity cold damage increases to 2d6 and extends to 10 feet. And he gains an additional ability: at the start of each of his turns, he creates a 20-foot radius area of extreme cold centered on himself. Each creature in the area must make a DC 19 Constitution saving throw or take 3d6 cold damage and have its speed reduced by 10 feet until the end of its next turn.

After Blizzard Form ends, Midbus's cryogenic systems need time to recalibrate. For 1 minute following the transformation's end, his AC decreases by 4, he loses cold immunity (gaining only resistance), and his Frost Breath cannot recharge. This vulnerability period is the window during which skilled opponents can exploit the overclocked systems' aftermath.
description.chat: Ice builds around him in layers—thicker, colder, MORE—until what stands there isn't a pig-beast anymore but a walking blizzard with fists and the intent to use them.

description.value:
Midbus is immune to all magical effects that would compel him to act against Fawful's interests. Charm Person, Dominate Monster, Suggestion, magical persuasion of any kind—nothing works if the commanded action would harm Fawful, betray Fawful's plans, or compromise Fawful's objectives. This isn't magical protection; it's the absolute loyalty of a creature whose entire identity was constructed around service to one individual. Midbus doesn't resist control because he's protected. He resists because disobeying Fawful is literally inconceivable to him—the neural pathways for independent decision-making regarding Fawful simply don't exist.

This loyalty makes Midbus the most reliable enforcer in the current crisis. He will not betray. He will not negotiate. He will not change sides, accept bribes, or respond to appeals to self-interest because his self-interest IS Fawful's interest. The only circumstance under which this loyalty wavers is the Bowser rivalry, and even that waiver is temporary—after the fight ends, Midbus returns to Fawful's service without question.

The loyalty also represents Midbus's greatest weakness against parties who understand it. Midbus will follow Fawful's orders even when those orders are tactically unsound, because evaluating orders for soundness requires independent judgment that Midbus doesn't possess. Fawful's genius compensates for this limitation under normal circumstances, but if Fawful is incapacitated, distracted, or making mistakes due to his own emotional compromises (the Green Mustache grudge, for example), Midbus will execute bad orders with the same commitment he brings to good ones.
description.chat: He follows because following is what he is. Not what he does—what he IS. Remove Fawful and what remains isn't a rebel. It's a weapon without a hand to aim it.

description.value:
Midbus serves as garrison commander of Peach's Castle, managing 500+ troops through a command style that prioritizes simplicity over sophistication. His orders are clear, his expectations are straightforward, and his consequences for failure are painful. This approach produces a garrison that is disciplined through fear rather than loyalty, competent at following instructions but incapable of independent adaptation when instructions don't cover the situation.

As a bonus action, Midbus can issue a command to garrison soldiers within 60 feet. Soldiers who hear the command gain advantage on their next attack roll or saving throw as they respond to their commander's direction with the urgent compliance of people who know what happens when Midbus is disappointed.

Midbus's garrison management has one significant blind spot: he doesn't look for infiltrators. Servants, maintenance workers, and support staff are beneath his notice. He focuses on soldiers because soldiers are what he understands. The HOMECOMING operatives embedded in Fawful's servant staff operate directly under his command structure, invisible because Midbus has never thought to question whether the people preparing his meals might have agendas beyond food preparation.
description.chat: He commands through the simplest possible principle: do what I say or I will make you wish you had. The principle works. The blind spots it creates might get him killed.

description.value: Twice per day, when Midbus fails a saving throw, he can choose to succeed instead. His modified physiology and the cryogenic systems' integration with his nervous system provide resilience against effects that would stop organic creatures. He pushes through magical compulsion through stubbornness rather than sophistication—his mind is too simple to be redirected and too committed to be overridden.
description.chat: The spell hits. The spell should work. Midbus doesn't care about should. Midbus shrugs it off and keeps coming.

description.value:
Midbus can take 3 legendary actions, choosing from the options below. Only one legendary action can be used at a time and only at the end of another creature's turn.

Frost Stomp (1 action): Midbus stomps the ground, creating a 10-foot radius of ice centered on himself. Each creature in the area must succeed on a DC 17 Dexterity saving throw or fall prone. The ice persists as difficult terrain for 1 round.

Ice Throw (1 action): Midbus tears a chunk of ice from his own armor and hurls it at a target within 60 feet. Ranged attack: +11 to hit, 2d8 + 7 bludgeoning damage plus 1d8 cold damage.

Charge (2 actions): Midbus moves up to his speed toward a target and makes one Blizzard Fist attack at the end of the movement. If the attack hits, the target must succeed on a DC 19 Strength saving throw or be knocked prone.

Frozen Rage (3 actions): Midbus plants himself and swings his fists in a 15-foot radius around himself. Each creature in the area must make a DC 19 Dexterity saving throw, taking 2d10 + 7 bludgeoning damage plus 2d8 cold damage on a failure, or half on a success. After using this action, Midbus cannot take legendary actions until the start of his next turn.
description.chat: Between other creatures' turns, the ice moves—stomping, throwing, charging, raging—a frozen engine of violence that doesn't wait for its own turn to cause destruction.

description.value:
If Fawful is killed, incapacitated, or otherwise removed from the picture, Midbus does not adapt. He does not develop independent objectives. He does not become his own agent. He becomes a weapon without a wielder—still dangerous, still powerful, but without direction, without purpose, without the organizing intelligence that transformed him from animal into enforcer.

Without Fawful's orders, Midbus defaults to the last instructions he received and follows them until they become impossible, then stands still and waits for new instructions that will never come. If no instructions are available, he reverts to territorial behavior: defending whatever location he's currently in against all comers, attacking anything that enters his space, eating whatever is available, and slowly becoming less and less distinguishable from the unintelligent beast he was before Fawful found him.

This regression is neither instant nor inevitable—if someone else assumes command authority that Midbus accepts (which would require either fooling him into believing they speak for Fawful or demonstrating power sufficient to establish new loyalty), he could be redirected. But establishing new loyalty in a creature whose identity is built around one specific person is extraordinarily difficult. Fawful didn't just give Midbus orders. Fawful gave Midbus a SELF. Without Fawful, the self dissolves, and what remains is meat and ice and nothing else.
description.chat: Without the mind that aimed him, the weapon doesn't rebel. It doesn't adapt. It simply stops being a weapon and starts being a thing—large, cold, and waiting for someone who isn't coming back.

The ghost enters the Ethereal Plane from the Material Plane, or vice versa. It is visible on the Material Plane while it is in the Border Ethereal, and vice versa, yet it can't affect or be affected by anything on the other plane.

Each non-undead creature within 60 ft. of the ghost that can see it must succeed on a DC 13 Wisdom saving throw or be frightened for 1 minute. If the save fails by 5 or more, the target also ages 1d4 x 10 years.

A frightened target can repeat the saving throw at the end of each of its turns, ending the frightened condition on itself on a success. If a target's saving throw is successful or the effect ends for it, the target is immune to this ghost's Horrifying Visage for the next 24 hours. The aging effect can be reversed with a greater restoration spell, but only within 24 hours of it occurring.

Each non-undead creature within 60 ft. of the ghost that can see it must succeed make a Wisdom saving throw. A target can repeat the saving throw at the end of each of its turns, ending the condition on itself on a success.

One humanoid that the ghost can see within 5 ft. of it must succeed on a DC 13 Charisma saving throw or be possessed by the ghost; the ghost then disappears, and the target is incapacitated and loses control of its body. The ghost now controls the body but doesn't deprive the target of awareness.

The ghost can't be targeted by any attack, spell, or other effect, except ones that turn undead, and it retains its alignment, Intelligence, Wisdom, Charisma, and immunity to being charmed and frightened. It otherwise uses the possessed target's statistics, but doesn't gain access to the target's knowledge, class features, or proficiencies.The possession lasts until the body drops to 0 hit points, the ghost ends it as a bonus action, or the ghost is turned or forced out by an effect like the dispel evil and good spell. When the possession ends, the ghost reappears in an unoccupied space within 5 ft. of the body. The target is immune to this ghost's Possession for 24 hours after succeeding on the saving throw or after the possession ends.

One humanoid that the ghost can see within 5 ft. of it must make a Charisma saving throw.

Masters of invention, artificers use ingenuity and magic to unlock extraordinary capabilities in objects. They see magic as a complex system waiting to be decoded and then harnessed in their spells and inventions. You can find everything you need to play one of these inventors in the next few sections. Artificers use a variety of tools to channel their arcane power. To cast a spell, an artificer might use alchemist's supplies to create a potent elixir, calligrapher's supplies to inscribe a sigil of power, or tinker's tools to craft a temporary charm. The magic of artificers is tied to their tools and their talents, and few other characters can produce the right tool for a job as well as an artificer.

Artificers in Many Worlds

Throughout the D&D multiverse, artificers create inventions and magic items of peace and war. Many lives have been brightened or saved because of the work of kind artificers, but countless lives have also been lost because of the mass destruction unleashed by certain artificers' creations.

In the Forgotten Realms, the island of Lantan is home to many artificers, and in the world of Dragonlance, tinker gnomes are often members of this class. The strange technologies in the Barrier Peaks of the world of Greyhawk have inspired some folk to walk the path of the artificer, and in Mystara, various nations employ artificers to keep airships and other wondrous devices operational.

Artificers in the City of Sigil share discoveries from throughout the multiverse, and from there, the gnome artificer Vi runs a cosmos-spanning business that hires adventurers to fix problems that others deem unfixable. In Vi's home world, Eberron, magic is harnessed as a form of science and deployed throughout society, largely as a result of the wondrous ingenuity of artificers.

Creating an Artificer

To create an artificer, consult the subsections which give you hit points, proficiencies, and starting equipment. Then look at the Artificer table to see which features you get at each level. The descriptions of those features appear below.

“Artificers invent cutting-edge problems, then try to solve them-loudly and often with collateral damage.”

— Tasha

Multiclassing and the Artificer

If your group uses the optional rule on multiclassing in the Player's Handbook, here's what you need to know if you choose artificer as one of your classes.

Ability Score Minimum. As a multiclass character, you must have at least an Intelligence score of 13 to take a level in this class, or to take a level in another class if you are already an artificer.

Proficiencies Gained. If artificer isn't your initial class, here are the proficiencies you gain when you take your first level as an artificer: light armor, medium armor, shields, @item[thieves' tools|PHB], @item[tinker's tools|PHB].

Spell Slots. Add half your levels (rounded up) in the artificer class to the appropriate levels from other classes to determine your available spell slots.

Artificer

Masters of unlocking magic in everyday objects, artificers are supreme inventors. They see magic as a complex system waiting to be decoded and controlled. Artificers use tools to channel arcane power, crafting magical objects. To cast a spell, an artificer could use @item[alchemist's supplies|PHB] to create a potent elixir, @item[calligrapher's supplies|PHB] to inscribe a sigil of power on an ally's armor, or @item[tinker's tools|PHB] to craft a temporary charm. The magic of artificers is tied to their tools and their talents.

Arcane Science

In the world of Eberron, arcane magic has been harnessed as a form of science and deployed throughout society. Artificers reflect this development. Their knowledge of magical devices, and their ability to infuse mundane items with magic, allows Eberron's most miraculous projects to continue.

During the Last War, artificers were marshaled on a massive scale. Many lives were saved because of the inventions of brave artificers, but countless lives were also lost because of the mass destruction unleashed by their creations.

Seekers of New Lore

Nothing excites an artificer quite like uncovering a new metal or discovering a source of elemental energy. In artificer circles, new inventions and strange discoveries create the most excitement. Artificers who wish to make their mark must innovate, creating something fresh, rather than iterating on familiar designs.

This drive for novelty pushes artificers to become adventurers. Eberron's main travel routes and populated regions have long since been explored. Thus, artificers seek the frontiers of civilization in hopes of making the next great discovery in arcane research.

Creating an Artificer

When creating an artificer, think about your character's relationship with the artisan who taught them their craft. Does the character have a rival? Talk to your DM about the role played by artificers in the campaign and the sort of organizations you might have ties to.

Artificers in Other Worlds

Eberron is the world most associated with artificers, yet the class can be found throughout the D&D multiverse. In the Forgotten Realms, for example, the island of Lantan is home to many artificers, and in the world of Dragonlance, tinker gnomes are often members of this class. The strange technologies in the Barrier Peaks of the World of Greyhawk have inspired some folk to walk the path of the artificer, and in Mystara, various nations employ artificers to keep airships and other wondrous devices operational. In the City of Sigil, artificers share discoveries from throughout the cosmos, and one in particular—the gnome inventor Vi—has run a multiverse-spanning business from there since leaving the world of her birth, Eberron. In the world-city Ravnica, the Izzet League trains numerous artificers, the destructiveness of whom is unparalleled in other worlds—except, perhaps, by the tinker gnomes of Krynn.

Quick Build

You can make an artificer quickly by following these suggestions. First, put your highest ability score in Intelligence, followed by Constitution or Dexterity. Second, choose the @background[guild artisan] background.

Level 1: Optional Rule: Firearm Proficiency

The secrets of creating and operating gunpowder weapons have been discovered in various corners of the D&D multiverse. If your Dungeon Master uses the rules on firearms in chapter 9 of the Dungeon Master's Guide and your artificer has been exposed to the operation of such weapons, your artificer is proficient with them.

Level 1: Magical Tinkering

1st-level artificer feature

You've learned how to invest a spark of magic into mundane objects. To use this ability, you must have @item[thieves' tools|PHB] or @item[artisan's tools|PHB] in hand. You then touch a Tiny nonmagical object as an action and give it one of the following magical properties of your choice:

  • The object sheds bright light in a 5-foot radius and dim light for an additional 5 feet.
  • Whenever tapped by a creature, the object emits a recorded message that can be heard up to 10 feet away. You utter the message when you bestow this property on the object, and the recording can be no more than 6 seconds long.
  • The object continuously emits your choice of an odor or a nonverbal sound (wind, waves, chirping, or the like). The chosen phenomenon is perceivable up to 10 feet away.
  • A static visual effect appears on one of the object's surfaces. This effect can be a picture, up to 25 words of text, lines and shapes, or a mixture of these elements, as you like.

The chosen property lasts indefinitely. As an action, you can touch the object and end the property early.

You can bestow magic on multiple objects, touching one object each time you use this feature, though a single object can only bear one property at a time. The maximum number of objects you can affect with this feature at one time is equal to your Intelligence modifier (minimum of one object). If you try to exceed your maximum, the oldest property immediately ends, and then the new property applies.

Level 1: Spellcasting

1st-level artificer feature

You've studied the workings of magic and how to cast spells, channeling the magic through objects. To observers, you don't appear to be casting spells in a conventional way; you appear to produce wonders from mundane items and outlandish inventions.

Tools Required

You produce your artificer spell effects through your tools. You must have a spellcasting focus—specifically @item[thieves' tools|phb] or some kind of @item[artisan's tools|phb|artisan's tool]—in hand when you cast any spell with this Spellcasting feature (meaning the spell has an 'M' component when you cast it). You must be proficient with the tool to use it in this way. See chapter 5, "Equipment," in the Player's Handbook for descriptions of these tools.

After you gain the Infuse Item feature at 2nd level, you can also use any item bearing one of your infusions as a spellcasting focus.

The Magic of Artifice

As an artificer, you use tools when you cast your spells. When describing your spellcasting, think about how you're using a tool to perform the spell effect. If you cast @spell[cure wounds] using @item[alchemist's supplies|PHB], you could be quickly producing a salve. If you cast it using @item[tinker's tools|PHB], you might have a miniature mechanical spider that binds wounds. When you cast @spell[poison spray], you could fling foul chemicals or use a wand that spits venom. The effect of the spell is the same as for a spellcaster of any other class, but your method of spellcasting is special.

The same principle applies when you prepare your spells. As an artificer, you don't study a spellbook or pray to prepare your spells. Instead, you work with your tools and create the specialized items you'll use to produce your effects. If you replace @spell[cure wounds] with @spell[heat metal], you might be altering the device you use to heal—perhaps modifying a tool so that it channels heat instead of healing energy.

Such details don't limit you in any way or provide you with any benefit beyond the spell's effects. You don't have to justify how you're using tools to cast a spell. But describing your spellcasting creatively is a fun way to distinguish yourself from other spellcasters.

Cantrips (0-Level Spells)

At 1st level, you know two cantrips of your choice from the artificer spell list. At higher levels, you learn additional artificer cantrips of your choice, as shown in the Cantrips Known column of the Artificer table.

When you gain a level in this class, you can replace one of the artificer cantrips you know with another cantrip from the artificer spell list.

Preparing and Casting Spells

The Artificer table shows how many spell slots you have to cast your artificer spells. To cast one of your artificer spells of 1st level or higher, you must expend a slot of the spell's level or higher. You regain all expended spell slots when you finish a long rest.

You prepare the list of artificer spells that are available for you to cast, choosing from the artificer spell list. When you do so, choose a number of artificer spells equal to your Intelligence modifier + half your artificer level, rounded down (minimum of one spell). The spells must be of a level for which you have spell slots.

For example, if you are a 5th-level artificer, you have four 1st-level and two 2nd-level spell slots. With an Intelligence of 14, your list of prepared spells can include four spells of 1st or 2nd level, in any combination. If you prepare the 1st-level spell @spell[cure wounds], you can cast it using a 1st-level or a 2nd-level slot. Casting the spell doesn't remove it from your list of prepared spells.

You can change your list of prepared spells when you finish a long rest. Preparing a new list of artificer spells requires time spent tinkering with your spellcasting focuses: at least 1 minute per spell level for each spell on your list.

Spellcasting Ability

Intelligence is your spellcasting ability for your artificer spells; your understanding of the theory behind magic allows you to wield these spells with superior skill. You use your Intelligence whenever an artificer spell refers to your spellcasting ability. In addition, you use your Intelligence modifier when setting the saving throw DC for an artificer spell you cast and when making an attack roll with one.

Spell save DC = 8 + Intelligence modifier + Proficiency Bonus
Spell attack modifier = Intelligence modifier + Proficiency Bonus

Ritual Casting

You can cast an artificer spell as a ritual if that spell has the ritual tag and you have the spell prepared.

Level 2: Infuse Item

2nd-level artificer feature

You've gained the ability to imbue mundane items with certain magical infusions, turning those objects into magic items.

Infusions Known

When you gain this feature, pick four artificer infusions to learn, choosing from the "Artificer Infusions" section at the end of the class's description. You learn additional infusions of your choice when you reach certain levels in this class, as shown in the Infusions Known column of the Artificer table.

Whenever you gain a level in this class, you can replace one of the artificer infusions you learned with a new one.

Artificer Infusions

Artificers have invented numerous magical infusions, extraordinary processes that rapidly create magic items. To many, artificers seem like wonderworkers, accomplishing in hours what others need weeks to complete.

The description of each of the following infusions details the type of item that can receive it, along with whether the resulting magic item requires attunement.

Some infusions specify a minimum artificer level. You can't learn such an infusion until you are at least that level.

Unless an infusion's description says otherwise, you can't learn an infusion more than once.

Infusing an Item

Whenever you finish a long rest, you can touch a nonmagical object and imbue it with one of your artificer infusions, turning it into a magic item. An infusion works on only certain kinds of objects, as specified in the infusion's description. If the item requires attunement, you can attune yourself to it the instant you infuse the item. If you decide to attune to the item later, you must do so using the normal process for attunement (see "Attunement" in chapter 7 of the Dungeon Master's Guide).

Your infusion remains in an item indefinitely, but when you die, the infusion vanishes after a number of days have passed equal to your Intelligence modifier (minimum of 1 day). The infusion also vanishes if you give up your knowledge of the infusion for another one.

You can infuse more than one nonmagical object at the end of a long rest; the maximum number of objects appears in the Infused Items column of the Artificer table. You must touch each of the objects, and each of your infusions can be in only one object at a time. Moreover, no object can bear more than one of your infusions at a time. If you try to exceed your maximum number of infusions, the oldest infusion immediately ends, and then the new infusion applies.

If an infusion ends on an item that contains other things, like a @item[bag of holding], its contents harmlessly appear in and around its space.

Level 3: Artificer Specialist

3rd-level artificer feature

Choose the type of specialist you are, each of which is detailed at the end of the class's description. Your choice grants you features at 5th level and again at 9th and 15th level.

Level 3: The Right Tool for the Job

3rd-level artificer feature

You've learned how to produce exactly the tool you need: with @item[thieves' tools|PHB] or @item[artisan's tools|PHB] in hand, you can magically create one set of @item[artisan's tools|PHB] in an unoccupied space within 5 feet of you. This creation requires 1 hour of uninterrupted work, which can coincide with a short or long rest. Though the product of magic, the tools are nonmagical, and they vanish when you use this feature again.

Level 4: Ability Score Improvement

4th-level artificer feature

When you reach 4th level, you can increase one ability score of your choice by 2, or you can increase two ability scores of your choice by 1. As normal, you can't increase an ability score above 20 using this feature.

If your DM allows the use of feats, you may instead take a feat.

Level 5: Artificer Specialist Feature

5th-level artificer feature

You gain a feature granted by your Artificer Specialist choice.

Level 6: Tool Expertise

6th-level artificer feature

Your proficiency bonus is now doubled for any ability check you make that uses your proficiency with a tool.

Level 7: Flash of Genius

7th-level artificer feature

You've gained the ability to come up with solutions under pressure. When you or another creature you can see within 30 feet of you makes an ability check or a saving throw, you can use your reaction to add your Intelligence modifier to the roll.

You can use this feature a number of times equal to your Intelligence modifier (minimum of once). You regain all expended uses when you finish a long rest.

Level 8: Ability Score Improvement

8th-level artificer feature

When you reach 8th level, you can increase one ability score of your choice by 2, or you can increase two ability scores of your choice by 1. As normal, you can't increase an ability score above 20 using this feature.

If your DM allows the use of feats, you may instead take a feat.

Level 9: Artificer Specialist Feature

9th-level artificer feature

You gain a feature granted by your Artificer Specialist choice.

Level 10: Magic Item Adept

10th-level artificer feature

You've achieved a profound understanding of how to use and make magic items:

  • You can attune to up to four magic items at once.
  • If you craft a magic item with a rarity of common or uncommon, it takes you a quarter of the normal time, and it costs you half as much of the usual gold.

Level 11: Spell-Storing Item

11th-level artificer feature

You can now store a spell in an object. Whenever you finish a long rest, you can touch one simple or martial weapon or one item that you can use as a spellcasting focus, and you store a spell in it, choosing a 1st- or 2nd-level spell from the artificer spell list that requires 1 action to cast (you needn't have it prepared).

While holding the object, a creature can take an action to produce the spell's effect from it, using your spellcasting ability modifier. If the spell requires @status[concentration], the creature must concentrate. The spell stays in the object until it's been used a number of times equal to twice your Intelligence modifier (minimum of twice) or until you use this feature again to store a spell in an object.

Level 12: Ability Score Improvement

12th-level artificer feature

When you reach 12th level, you can increase one ability score of your choice by 2, or you can increase two ability scores of your choice by 1. As normal, you can't increase an ability score above 20 using this feature.

If your DM allows the use of feats, you may instead take a feat.

Level 14: Magic Item Savant

14th-level artificer feature

Your skill with magic items deepens:

  • You can attune to up to five magic items at once.
  • You ignore all class, race, spell, and level requirements on attuning to or using a magic item.

Level 15: Artificer Specialist Feature

15th-level artificer feature

You gain a feature granted by your Artificer Specialist choice.

Level 16: Ability Score Improvement

16th-level artificer feature

When you reach 16th level, you can increase one ability score of your choice by 2, or you can increase two ability scores of your choice by 1. As normal, you can't increase an ability score above 20 using this feature.

If your DM allows the use of feats, you may instead take a feat.

Level 18: Magic Item Master

18th-level artificer feature

You can now attune to up to six magic items at once.

Level 19: Ability Score Improvement

19th-level artificer feature

When you reach 19th level, you can increase one ability score of your choice by 2, or you can increase two ability scores of your choice by 1. As normal, you can't increase an ability score above 20 using this feature.

If your DM allows the use of feats, you may instead take a feat.

Level 20: Soul of Artifice

20th-level artificer feature

You have developed a mystical connection to your magic items, which you can draw on for protection:

  • You gain a +1 bonus to all saving throws per magic item you are currently attuned to.
  • If you're reduced to 0 hit points but not killed outright, you can use your reaction to end one of your artificer infusions, causing you to drop to 1 hit point instead of 0.

Battle Smith

Armies require protection, and someone has to put things back together if defenses fail. A combination of protector and medic, a Battle Smith is an expert at defending others and repairing both material and personnel. To aid in their work, Battle Smiths are usually accompanied by a steel defender, a protective companion of their own creation. Many soldiers tell stories of nearly dying before being saved by a Battle Smith and a steel defender.

Battle Smiths played a key role in House Cannith's work on battle constructs and the original warforged, and after the Last War, these artificers led efforts to aid those who were injured in the war's horrific battles.

When you adopt this specialization at 3rd level, you gain proficiency with @item[smith's tools|PHB]. If you already have this proficiency, you gain proficiency with one other type of @item[artisan's tools|PHB] of your choice.

Level 3: Battle Smith Spells

Starting at 3rd level, you always have certain spells prepared after you reach particular levels in this class, as shown in the Battle Smith Spells table. These spells count as artificer spells for you, but they don't count against the number of artificer spells you prepare.

Level 3: Battle Ready

When you reach 3rd level, your combat training and your experiments with magic have paid off in two ways:

  • You gain proficiency with martial weapons.
  • When you attack with a magic weapon, you can use your Intelligence modifier, instead of Strength or Dexterity modifier, for the attack and damage rolls.

Level 3: Steel Defender

By 3rd level, your tinkering has borne you a faithful companion, a @creature[steel defender|tce]. It is friendly to you and your companions, and it obeys your commands. See this creature's game statistics in the steel defender stat block, which uses your proficiency bonus (PB) in several places. You determine the creature's appearance and whether it has two legs or four; your choice has no effect on its game statistics.

In combat, the defender shares your initiative count, but it takes its turn immediately after yours. It can move and use its reaction on its own, but the only action it takes on its turn is the @action[Dodge] action, unless you take a bonus action on your turn to command it to take another action. That action can be one in its stat block or some other action. If you are &Reference[condition=incapacitated], the defender can take any action of its choice, not just @action[Dodge].

If the @spell[mending] spell is cast on it, it regains [[/r 2d6]] hit points. If it has died within the last hour, you can use your @item[smith's tools|PHB] as an action to revive it, provided you are within 5 feet of it and you expend a spell slot of 1st level or higher. The steel defender returns to life after 1 minute with all its hit points restored.

At the end of a long rest, you can create a new steel defender if you have your @item[smith's tools|PHB] with you. If you already have a steel defender from this feature, the first one immediately perishes. The defender also perishes if you die.

Level 5: Extra Attack

Starting at 5th level, you can attack twice, rather than once, whenever you take the @action[Attack] action on your turn.

Level 9: Arcane Jolt

At 9th level, you learn new ways to channel arcane energy to harm or heal. When either you hit a target with a magic weapon attack or your steel defender hits a target, you can channel magical energy through the strike to create one of the following effects:

  • The target takes an extra [[/damage 2d6 type=force]] damage.
  • Choose one creature or object you can see within 30 feet of the target. Healing energy flows into the chosen recipient, restoring [[/r 2d6]] hit points to it.

You can use this energy a number of times equal to your Intelligence modifier (minimum of once), but you can do so no more than once on a turn. You regain all expended uses when you finish a long rest.

Level 15: Improved Defender

At 15th level, your Arcane Jolt and steel defender become more powerful:

  • The extra damage and the healing of your Arcane Jolt both increase to [[/damage 4d6]].
  • Your steel defender gains a +2 bonus to Armor Class.
  • Whenever your steel defender uses its Deflect Attack, the attacker takes force damage equal to [[/damage 1d4]] + your Intelligence modifier.

It takes 10 minutes to recover the Caltrops.
Using a Crowbar gives you @variantrule[Advantage|XPHB] on Strength checks where the Crowbar's leverage can be applied.

You can douse a creature, object, or space with Oil or use it as fuel, as detailed below.

Dousing a Creature or an Object. When you take the @action[Attack|XPHB] action, you can replace one of your attacks with throwing an Oil flask. Target one creature or object within 20 feet of yourself. The target must succeed on a Dexterity saving throw (DC 8 plus your Dexterity modifier and @variantrule[Proficiency|XPHB|Proficiency Bonus]) or be covered in oil. If the target takes Fire damage before the oil dries (after 1 minute), the target takes an extra 5 Fire damage from burning oil.

Dousing a Space. You can take the @action[Utilize|XPHB] action to pour an Oil flask on level ground to cover a 5-foot-square area within 5 feet of yourself. If lit, the oil burns until the end of the turn 2 rounds from when the oil was lit (or 12 seconds) and deals 5 Fire damage to any creature that enters the area or ends its turn there. A creature can take this damage only once per turn.

Fuel. Oil serves as fuel for Lamps and Lanterns. Once lit, a flask of Oil burns for 6 hours in a Lamp or Lantern. That duration doesn't need to be consecutive; you can extinguish the burning Oil (as a @action[Utilize|XPHB] action) and rekindle it again until it has burned for a total of 6 hours.

As a @action[Utilize|XPHB] action, you can tie a knot with Rope if you succeed on a DC 10 Dexterity (&Reference[skill=SleightofHand]{Sleight of Hand}) check. The Rope can be burst with a successful DC 20 Strength (&Reference[skill=Athletics]) check.

You can bind an unwilling creature with the Rope only if the creature has the &Reference[condition=Grappled], &Reference[condition=Incapacitated], or &Reference[condition=Restrained] condition. If the creature's legs are bound, the creature has the &Reference[condition=Restrained] condition until it escapes. Escaping the Rope requires the creature to make a successful DC 15 Dexterity (&Reference[skill=Acrobatics]) check as an action.

A Tinderbox is a small container holding flint, fire steel, and tinder (usually dry cloth soaked in light oil) used to kindle a fire. Using it to light a @item[Candle|XPHB], @item[Lamp|XPHB], @item[Hooded Lantern|XPHB|Lantern], or @item[Torch|XPHB]—or anything else with exposed fuel—takes a @variantrule[Bonus Action|XPHB]. Lighting any other fire takes 1 minute.

A Torch burns for 1 hour, casting @variantrule[Bright Light|XPHB] in a 20-foot radius and @variantrule[Dim Light|XPHB] for an additional 20 feet. When you take the @action[Attack|XPHB] action, you can attack with the Torch, using it as a Simple Melee weapon. On a hit, the target takes 1 Fire damage.

2nd-level artificer feature

You've gained the ability to imbue mundane items with certain magical infusions, turning those objects into magic items.

Artificer Infusions

Artificers have invented numerous magical infusions, extraordinary processes that rapidly create magic items. To many, artificers seem like wonderworkers, accomplishing in hours what others need weeks to complete.

The description of each of the following infusions details the type of item that can receive it, along with whether the resulting magic item requires attunement.

Some infusions specify a minimum artificer level. You can't learn such an infusion until you are at least that level.

Unless an infusion's description says otherwise, you can't learn an infusion more than once.

Infusing an Item

Whenever you finish a long rest, you can touch a nonmagical object and imbue it with one of your artificer infusions, turning it into a magic item. An infusion works on only certain kinds of objects, as specified in the infusion's description. If the item requires attunement, you can attune yourself to it the instant you infuse the item. If you decide to attune to the item later, you must do so using the normal process for attunement (see "Attunement" in chapter 7 of the Dungeon Master's Guide).

Your infusion remains in an item indefinitely, but when you die, the infusion vanishes after a number of days have passed equal to your Intelligence modifier (minimum of 1 day). The infusion also vanishes if you give up your knowledge of the infusion for another one.

You can infuse more than one nonmagical object at the end of a long rest; the maximum number of objects appears in the Infused Items column of the Artificer table. You must touch each of the objects, and each of your infusions can be in only one object at a time. Moreover, no object can bear more than one of your infusions at a time. If you try to exceed your maximum number of infusions, the oldest infusion immediately ends, and then the new infusion applies.

If an infusion ends on an item that contains other things, like a @item[bag of holding], its contents harmlessly appear in and around its space.

description.value:
You assume a different form. When you cast the spell, choose one of the following options, the effects of which last for the duration of the spell. While the spell lasts, you can end one option as an action to gain the benefits of a different one.

Aquatic Adaptation. You adapt your body to an aquatic environment, sprouting gills and growing webbing between your fingers. You can breathe underwater and gain a swimming speed equal to your walking speed.

Change Appearance. You transform your appearance. You decide what you look like, including your height, weight, facial features, sound of your voice, hair length, coloration, and distinguishing characteristics, if any. You can make yourself appear as a member of another race, though none of your statistics change. You also can't appear as a creature of a different size than you, and your basic shape stays the same; if you're bipedal, you can't use this spell to become quadrupedal, for instance. At any time for the duration of the spell, you can use your action to change your appearance in this way again.

Natural Weapons. You grow claws, fangs, spines, horns, or a different natural weapon of your choice. Your unarmed strikes deal [[/damage 1d6]] bludgeoning, piercing, or slashing damage, as appropriate to the natural weapon you chose, and you are proficient with your unarmed strikes. Finally, the natural weapon is magic and you have a +1 bonus to the attack and damage rolls you make using it.

You touch a closed door, window, gate, chest, or other entryway, and it becomes locked for the duration. You and the creatures you designate when you cast this spell can open the object normally. You can also set a password that, when spoken within 5 feet of the object, suppresses this spell for 1 minute. Otherwise, it is impassable until it is broken or the spell is dispelled or suppressed. Casting @spell[knock] on the object suppresses @spell[arcane lock] for 10 minutes.

While affected by this spell, the object is more difficult to break or force open; the DC to break it or pick any locks on it increases by 10.

Bear's Endurance. The target has advantage on Constitution checks. It also gains [[/r 2d6]] temporary hit points, which are lost when the spell ends.

Bull's Strength. The target has advantage on Strength checks, and his or her carrying capacity doubles.

Cat's Grace. The target has advantage on Dexterity checks. It also doesn't take damage from falling 20 feet or less if it isn't &Reference[condition=incapacitated].

Eagle's Splendor. The target has advantage on Charisma checks.

Fox's Cunning. The target has advantage on Intelligence checks.

Owl's Wisdom. The target has advantage on Wisdom checks.

At Higher Levels. When you cast this spell using a spell slot of 3rd level or higher, you can target one additional creature for each slot level above 2nd.

You cause a creature or an object you can see within range to grow larger or smaller for the duration. Choose either a creature or an object that is neither worn nor carried. If the target is unwilling, it can make a Constitution saving throw. On a success, the spell has no effect.

If the target is a creature, everything it is wearing and carrying changes size with it. Any item dropped by an affected creature returns to normal size at once.

Enlarge. The target's size doubles in all dimensions, and its weight is multiplied by eight. This growth increases its size by one category—from Medium to Large, for example. If there isn't enough room for the target to double its size, the creature or object attains the maximum possible size in the space available. Until the spell ends, the target also has advantage on Strength checks and Strength saving throws. The target's weapons also grow to match its new size. While these weapons are enlarged, the target's attacks with them deal [[/damage 1d4]] extra damage.

Reduce. The target's size is halved in all dimensions, and its weight is reduced to one-eighth of normal. This reduction decreases its size by one category—from Medium to Small, for example. Until the spell ends, the target also has disadvantage on Strength checks and Strength saving throws. The target's weapons also shrink to match its new size. While these weapons are reduced, the target's attacks with them deal [[/damage 1d4]] less damage (this can't reduce the damage below 1).

Choose a manufactured metal object, such as a metal weapon or a suit of heavy or medium metal armor, that you can see within range. You cause the object to glow red-hot. Any creature in physical contact with the object takes [[/damage 2d8 type=fire]] damage when you cast the spell. Until the spell ends, you can use a bonus action on each of your subsequent turns to cause this damage again.

If a creature is holding or wearing the object and takes the damage from it, the creature must succeed on a Constitution saving throw or drop the object if it can. If it doesn't drop the object, it has disadvantage on attack rolls and ability checks until the start of your next turn.

At Higher Levels. When you cast this spell using a spell slot of 3rd level or higher, the damage increases by [[/damage 1d8]] for each slot level above 2nd.

The target can move only by pushing or pulling against a fixed object or surface within reach (such as a wall or a ceiling), which allows it to move as if it were climbing. You can change the target's altitude by up to 20 feet in either direction on your turn. If you are the target, you can move up or down as part of your move. When the spell ends, the target floats gently to the ground if it is still aloft.

You implant a message within an object in range, a message that is uttered when a trigger condition is met. Choose an object that you can see and that isn't being worn or carried by another creature. Then speak the message, which must be 25 words or less, though it can be delivered over as long as 10 minutes. Finally, determine the circumstance that will trigger the spell to deliver your message.

When that circumstance occurs, a magical mouth appears on the object and recites the message in your voice and at the same volume you spoke. If the object you chose has a mouth or something that looks like a mouth (for example, the mouth of a statue), the magical mouth appears there so that the words appear to come from the object's mouth. When you cast this spell, you can have the spell end after it delivers its message, or it can remain and repeat its message whenever the trigger occurs.

The triggering circumstance can be as general or as detailed as you like, though it must be based on visual or audible conditions that occur within 30 feet of the object. For example, you could instruct the mouth to speak when any creature moves within 30 feet of the object or when a silver bell rings within 30 feet of it.

You touch a length of rope that is up to 60 feet long. One end of the rope then rises into the air until the whole rope hangs perpendicular to the ground. At the upper end of the rope, an invisible entrance opens to an extradimensional space that lasts until the spell ends.

The extradimensional space can be reached by climbing to the top of the rope. The space can hold as many as eight Medium or smaller creatures. The rope can be pulled into the space, making the rope disappear from view outside the space.

Attacks and spells can't cross through the entrance into or out of the extradimensional space, but those inside can see out of it as if through a 3-foot-by-5-foot window centered on the rope.

Anything inside the extradimensional space drops out when the spell ends.

You conjure a mass of thick, sticky webbing at a point of your choice within range. The webs fill a 20-foot cube from that point for the duration. The webs are &Reference[rule=difficultterrain]{difficult terrain} and lightly obscure their area.

If the webs aren't anchored between two solid masses (such as walls or trees) or layered across a floor, wall, or ceiling, the conjured web collapses on itself, and the spell ends at the start of your next turn. Webs layered over a flat surface have a depth of 5 feet.

Each creature that starts its turn in the webs or that enters them during its turn must make a Dexterity saving throw. On a failed save, the creature is &Reference[condition=restrained] as long as it remains in the webs or until it breaks free.

A creature &Reference[condition=restrained] by the webs can use its action to make a Strength check against your spell save DC. If it succeeds, it is no longer &Reference[condition=restrained].

The webs are flammable. Any 5-foot cube of webs exposed to fire burns away in 1 round, dealing [[/damage 2d4 type=fire]] damage to any creature that starts its turn in the fire.

You magically empower your movement with dance-like steps, giving yourself the following benefits for the duration.

  • Your walking speed increases by 10 feet.
  • You don't provoke opportunity attacks.
  • You can move through the space of another creature, and it doesn't count as &Reference[rule=difficultterrain]{difficult terrain}. If you end your turn in another creature's space, you are shunted to the last unoccupied space you occupied, and you take [[/damage 1d8 type=force]] damage.

You magically twist space around another creature you can see within range. The target must succeed on a Constitution saving throw (the target can choose to fail), or the target is teleported to an unoccupied space of your choice that you can see within range. The chosen space must be on a surface or in a liquid that can support the target without the target having to squeeze.

If an effect would move either you or the weapon more than 30 feet away from each other, the other is dragged along as well.

You gain a +2 to attack and damage rolls made with this magic weapon. It has the thrown property with a normal range of 10 feet and a long range of 30 feet.

Immediately after making a ranged attack with this weapon on your turn, you can use a bonus action to reel the weapon back to your hand. The target of the attack must make a DC 17 Strength saving throw. On a failed save, the target is dragged up to 10 feet toward you if it is Large or smaller, or knocked &Reference[condition=prone] if it is Huge or larger.

Curse. This maul is cursed, and becoming attuned to it extends the curse to you. As long as you remain cursed, the weapon's chain binding it to you can't be removed, and you have disadvantage on attack rolls with weapons other than this one.

If you have a Strength score below 17, your movement speed is reduced by 20 feet and you have disadvantage on ability checks, attack rolls, and saving throws that use Strength, Dexterity, or Constitution while the weapon is bound to you.
